- [concept] Deep Agents is a complete agent harness with planning, subagents, a virtual filesystem, and long-term memory built in. — https://docs.langchain.com/build-overview
- [fact] Deep Agents is described as the fastest way to start building agents for complex, long-running tasks. — https://docs.langchain.com/build-overview
- [concept] LangChain is a minimal, configurable agent framework that allows composing exactly what you need from models, tools, prompts, and middleware. — https://docs.langchain.com/build-overview
- [concept] LangGraph provides low-level orchestration for stateful, long-running agents featuring durable execution, streaming, memory, and human-in-the-loop. — https://docs.langchain.com/build-overview
- [concept] Deep Agents Code is an open source terminal coding agent (dcode) built on the Deep Agents SDK. — https://docs.langchain.com/build-overview
- [fact] The dcode agent allows switching models mid-session, customizing skills and memory, and approving shell execution from the CLI. — https://docs.langchain.com/build-overview
- [concept] Integrations allow connecting to model providers, vector stores, retrievers, and other components. — https://docs.langchain.com/build-overview
- [fact] Python and TypeScript both support Deep Agents, LangChain, and LangGraph with identical feature descriptions for each framework. — https://docs.langchain.com/build-overview

- [definition] Attribute-based access control — This reference explains LangSmith's Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) system, which enables fine-grained access control based on resource attributes, complementing [RBAC](/langsmith/rbac). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#attribute-based-access-control
- [definition] Enable ABAC for self-hosted deployments — 1. ABAC requires a [self-hosted](/langsmith/self-hosted) LangSmith deployment running Helm chart 0.11.28 or later (application version 0.12.1). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#enable-abac-for-self-hosted-deployments
- [definition] Access policy structure — An access policy defines conditions under which access is granted or denied. Here's the structure: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#access-policy-structure
- [definition] Effect — The `effect` determines what happens when conditions match: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#effect
- [definition] Condition groups — The `condition_groups` array contains one or more condition groups. Multiple condition groups are evaluated with **OR logic** - if any group matches, the policy applies. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#condition-groups
- [definition] Roles — The `role_ids` array specifies which workspace roles the policy applies to. When a user with that role accesses a resource, the policy conditions are evaluated. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#roles
- [definition] Managing access policies — Access policies are managed via the LangSmith API by [Organization Admins](/langsmith/rbac#organization-admin). Before creating policies, [set up resource tags](/langsmith/set-up-resource-tags) in your workspace. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#managing-access-policies
- [definition] How ABAC works with RBAC — [RBAC](/langsmith/rbac) permissions and ABAC policies are both considered when determining access to resources: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#how-abac-works-with-rbac
- [definition] 1. Annotator team assignment — Allow annotators to only access datasets tagged for their team: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#1-annotator-team-assignment
- [definition] 2. Block sensitive data — Deny access to datasets containing PII. Since deny policies override allow policies, this blocks access even for users with RBAC permissions: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#2-block-sensitive-data
- [definition] 3. Application-based access with wildcards — Allow engineers to access projects for any application in the "chatbot" family using glob patterns: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#3-application-based-access-with-wildcards
- [definition] 4. Client and purpose isolation (AND logic) — Grant access only if both conditions are met - dataset is for training AND belongs to a specific client: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#4-client-and-purpose-isolation-and-logic
- [definition] 5. Client data plus resources without a `Client` tag using `_if_exists` — Consultants don't have RBAC `datasets:read` permission, but this policy grants them access to datasets tagged `Client=Acme-Corp`, as well as datasets that don't have a `Client` tag at all. Datasets tagged with a different client (e.g., `Client=Other-Corp`) remain blocked: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#5-client-data-plus-resources-without-a-client-tag-using-if-exists
- [definition] Tag resources at creation time — When ABAC policies are active, resources are access-controlled based on their tags. To make sure a resource is protected as soon as it is created, you can supply tags directly in the creation request using the `tag_value_ids` parameter. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/abac#tag-resources-at-creation-time

- [definition] Access the current run (span) within a traced function — In some cases you will want to access the current run (span) within a traced function. This can be useful for extracting UUIDs, tags, or other information from the current run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/access-current-span#access-the-current-run-span-within-a-traced-function
- [concept] You can access the current run (span) within a traced function to extract UUIDs, tags, or other information. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/access-current-span
- [fact] The `get_current_run_tree` function is used in the Python SDK to access the current run tree. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/access-current-span
- [fact] The `getCurrentRunTree` function is used in the TypeScript SDK to access the current run tree. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/access-current-span
- [concept] The `RunTree` object contains various properties that can be accessed once the current run is retrieved. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/access-current-span
- [actionable] Call `get_current_run_tree` in Python or `getCurrentRunTree` in TypeScript to retrieve the current run tree. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/access-current-span

- [concept] Static interrupts are triggered either before or after a node executes and are also known as static breakpoints. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/add-human-in-the-loop

- [concept] `interrupt_after` specifies the nodes where execution should pause after the node is executed. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/add-human-in-the-loop

- [definition] Overview — This overview covers topics related to managing users, organizations, workspaces, and applications within LangSmith. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#overview
- [definition] Organizations — An organization is a logical grouping of users within LangSmith that defines shared settings applying across all of its workspaces. These settings govern organization-wide concerns rather than individual projects within a workspace. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#organizations
- [definition] Workspaces — Workspaces were formerly called Tenants. Some code and APIs may still reference the old name for a period of time during the transition. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#workspaces
- [definition] Applications — An application is a logical grouping of resources within a workspace. Applications are often agents, but you can use them for any project within a team. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#applications
- [definition] Resources — Resources are the concrete entities used to build, run, and observe applications and agents, such as tracing projects, prompts, datasets, and deployments. Resources are scoped to a specific application. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#resources
- [definition] Additional info — The following diagram explains the relationship between organizations, workspaces, applications, and resources: ![Resource Hierarchy](/langsmith/images/resource-hierarchy.png) — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#additional-info
- [definition] Resource tags — Resource tags allow you to further segregate resources within a workspace for use with [ABAC](/langsmith/organization-workspace-operations#access-policies). Each tag is a key-value pair that you can assign to a resource. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#resource-tags
- [definition] Users — A user is a person who has access to LangSmith. Users can be members of one or more organizations and workspaces within those organizations. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#users
- [definition] API keys — We ended support for legacy API keys prefixed with `ls__` on October 22, 2024 in favor of personal access tokens (PATs) and service keys. We require using PATs and service keys for all new integrations. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#api-keys
- [definition] Organization roles — Organization roles are distinct from the [Enterprise feature workspace RBAC](#workspace-roles-rbac) and are used in the context of multiple [workspaces](#workspaces). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#organization-roles
- [definition] Workspace roles (RBAC) — RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is a feature that is only available to Enterprise customers. - [definition] Environment separation — Use [resource tags](#resource-tags) to organize resources by environment using the default tag key `Environment` and different values for the environment (e.g., `dev`, `staging`, `prod`). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#environment-separation
- [definition] Data retention — This section covers how data retention works and how it's priced in LangSmith. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#data-retention
- [definition] Rate limits — LangSmith has rate limits which are designed to ensure the stability of the service for all users. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#rate-limits
- [definition] Usage limits — LangSmith lets you configure usage limits on tracing. Note that these are *usage* limits, not *spend* limits, which mean they let you limit the quantity of occurrences of some event rather than the total amount you will spend. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#usage-limits

- [problem] Once an API key expires, it is no longer valid and cannot be reactivated or have its expiration modified. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#user-management-and-rbac
- [fact] PATs are scoped to a user and carry the same permissions as the user that created them. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#user-management-and-rbac

- [idea] Service keys are recommended for applications or services like LangGraph agents that need to interact with the LangSmith API. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#user-management-and-rbac
- [fact] Only admins can create service keys, which may be scoped to a single workspace, multiple workspaces, or the entire organization. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#user-management-and-rbac
- [problem] When using organization-scoped service keys, omitting the `X-Tenant-Id` header when accessing workspace-scoped resources results in a `403 Forbidden` error. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#user-management-and-rbac

- [fact] In Developer organizations with a single workspace, all users are assigned the Organization Admin role by default. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#user-management-and-rbac
- [concept] RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) is a feature available only to Enterprise customers for defining permissions within a workspace. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#user-management-and-rbac
- [fact] Workspace Admins have full access, Workspace Editors have full permissions except for workspace management, and Workspace Viewers have read-only access. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#user-management-and-rbac

- [idea] Do not use separate workspaces for environment separation because resources cannot be shared across them, which prevents promoting resources like prompts between environments. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#best-practices
- [concept] Resource tags are used to organize and filter resources such as tracing projects, datasets, and prompts within a workspace. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#best-practices
- [fact] Commit tags are labels that point to specific commits in a prompt's history to manage which version your code references. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#best-practices

- [concept] Resource tags determine which resources belong to an environment, while commit tags control which specific version of a prompt is referenced by code. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/administration-overview#best-practices

- [definition] Configure Agent Server for scale — The default configuration for the LangSmith Agent Server is designed to handle substantial read and write load across a variety of different workloads. By following the best practices outlined below, you can tune your Agent Server to perform optimally for your specific workload. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#configure-agent-server-for-scale
- [definition] Request vs. run concurrency — Two independent kinds of concurrency determine how the Agent Server scales, and they are controlled separately: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#request-vs-run-concurrency
- [definition] Write load — Write load is primarily driven by the following factors: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#write-load
- [definition] Tune `N_JOBS_PER_WORKER` based on assistant characteristics — The default value of [`N_JOBS_PER_WORKER`](/langsmith/env-var-self-hosted) is 10. You can change this value to scale the maximum number of runs that can be executed at a time by a single queue worker based on the characteristics of your assistant. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#tune-n-jobs-per-worker-based-on-assistant-characteristics
- [definition] Avoid synchronous blocking operations — Avoid synchronous blocking operations in your code and prefer asynchronous operations. Long synchronous operations can block the main event loop, causing longer request and run execution times and potential timeouts. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#avoid-synchronous-blocking-operations
- [definition] Minimize redundant checkpointing — Minimize redundant checkpointing by setting [`durability`](/oss/python/langgraph/checkpointers#durability-modes) to the minimum value necessary to ensure your data is durable. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#minimize-redundant-checkpointing
- [definition] Enable queue workers — By default, the API server manages the queue and does not use queue workers. Enable queue workers by setting `queue.enabled` to `true`: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#enable-queue-workers
- [definition] Size jobs for expected throughput — This section sizes run-execution capacity (queue workers), which is separate from request-serving capacity (API server replicas). For more information, see [Request vs. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#size-jobs-for-expected-throughput
- [definition] Configure autoscaling for bursty write workloads — Autoscaling is disabled by default, but should be configured for bursty workloads. Using the same calculations as the previous section, you can determine the maximum number of queue workers you should allow the autoscaler to scale to based on maximum expected throughput. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#configure-autoscaling-for-bursty-write-workloads
- [definition] Read load — Read load is primarily driven by the following factors: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#read-load
- [definition] Use filtering to reduce results per request — [Agent Server](/langsmith/agent-server) provides a search API for each resource type. These APIs implement pagination by default and offer many filtering options. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#use-filtering-to-reduce-results-per-request
- [definition] Set TTLs to automatically delete old data — Set a [TTL on threads](/langsmith/configure-ttl) to automatically clean up old data. Runs and checkpoints are automatically deleted when the associated thread is deleted. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#set-ttls-to-automatically-delete-old-data
- [definition] Avoid polling; use `/join` to monitor a run — Avoid polling the state of a run by using the `/join` API endpoint. This method returns the final state of the run once the run is complete. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#avoid-polling-use-join-to-monitor-a-run
- [definition] Configure autoscaling for bursty read workloads — Autoscaling is disabled by default, but should be configured for bursty workloads. Determine the maximum number of API servers you should allow the autoscaler to scale to based on maximum expected throughput. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#configure-autoscaling-for-bursty-read-workloads
- [definition] Example configurations — The exact optimal configuration depends on your application complexity, request patterns, and data requirements. Use the following examples in combination with the information in the previous sections and your specific usage to update your deployment configuration as needed. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#example-configurations
- [definition] Low reads, low writes — The default [LangSmith Deployment](/langsmith/deployment) configuration will handle this load. No custom resource configuration is needed here. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#low-reads-low-writes
- [definition] Low reads, high writes — You have a high volume of write requests (500 per second) being processed by your deployment, but relatively few read requests (5 per second). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#low-reads-high-writes
- [definition] High reads, low writes — You have a high volume of read requests (500 per second) but relatively few write requests (5 per second). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#high-reads-low-writes
- [definition] Medium reads, medium writes — This is a balanced configuration that should handle moderate read and write loads (50 read/50 write requests per second). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#medium-reads-medium-writes
- [definition] High reads, high writes — You have high volumes of both read and write requests (500 read/500 write requests per second). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#high-reads-high-writes
- [definition] Autoscaling — If your deployment experiences bursty traffic, you can enable autoscaling to scale the number of API servers and queue workers to handle the load. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server-scale#autoscaling

## Agent Server
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server>

- [snippet] Container architecture: flowchart TB — `flowchart TB` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server#container-architecture
- [definition] Agent Server — LangSmith Deployment's **Agent Server** offers an API for creating and managing agent-based applications. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server#agent-server
- [definition] Application structure — To deploy an Agent Server application, you need to specify the graph(s) you want to deploy, as well as any relevant configuration settings, such as dependencies and environment variables. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server#application-structure
- [definition] Parts of a deployment — When you deploy Agent Server, you are deploying one or more [graphs](#graphs), a database for [persistence](/oss/python/langgraph/persistence), and a [task queue](#task-queue). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server#parts-of-a-deployment
- [definition] Graphs — When you deploy a graph with Agent Server, you are deploying a "blueprint" for an [Assistant](/langsmith/assistants). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server#graphs
- [definition] Persistence — Agent Server persists three types of data, all backed by [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/) by default: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server#persistence
- [definition] Task queue — When a client creates a run, the API server enqueues it and a queue worker picks it up for execution. Workers can also be signaled to cancel a run in progress, and publish output events that open `/stream` connections forward to the client in real time. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server#task-queue
- [definition] Deployment modes — Agent Server supports three runtime configurations: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server#deployment-modes
- [definition] Container architecture — A typical deployment consists of two kinds of long-running containers, both built from the same Docker image (a base image with your project code installed on top): — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server#container-architecture
- [definition] Run execution lifecycle — When you invoke a run, the request flows through several components: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/agent-server#run-execution-lifecycle

- [definition] Feedback layers — LangSmith uses a three-layer architecture for structured human feedback: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#feedback-layers
- [definition] Create a feedback config — Feedback configs define the schema for a feedback key—whether it's a continuous score, a categorical choice, or freeform text. A unique key identifies each config within your organization and specifies how annotators can submit feedback for that metric. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#create-a-feedback-config
- [definition] List feedback configs — Retrieve feedback configs to see what evaluation criteria are available in your organization with [`list_feedback_configs`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langsmith/client/Client/list_feedback_configs). You can list all configs or filter by specific keys. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#list-feedback-configs
- [definition] Update a feedback config — Modify an existing feedback config with [`update_feedback_config`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langsmith/client/Client/update_feedback_config) by updating specific fields. The method only changes the fields you provide—the rest remain unchanged. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#update-a-feedback-config
- [definition] Delete a feedback config — Remove a feedback config from your organization with [`delete_feedback_config`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langsmith/client/Client/delete_feedback_config). This performs a soft delete, which marks the config as deleted but doesn't permanently remove it from the system. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#delete-a-feedback-config
- [definition] Annotation queue rubric items — Rubric items assign feedback configs to a specific annotation queue. They control which feedback forms annotators see when reviewing [runs](/langsmith/observability-concepts#runs) in that queue, and whether each form is required or optional. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#annotation-queue-rubric-items
- [definition] Create a queue with rubric items — Create an annotation queue with [`create_annotation_queue`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langsmith/client/Client/create_annotation_queue) and assign feedback configs to it through rubric items. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#create-a-queue-with-rubric-items
- [definition] Update rubric items on an existing queue — Modify the rubric items assigned to an annotation queue with [`update_annotation_queue`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langsmith/client/Client/update_annotation_queue). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#update-rubric-items-on-an-existing-queue
- [definition] Add runs and threads to a queue — Add [runs](/langsmith/observability-concepts#runs) and [threads](/langsmith/observability-concepts#threads) to a single-run annotation queue with the annotation queue `items` resource. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#add-runs-and-threads-to-a-queue
- [definition] Continuous — Continuous configs define numeric rating scales with minimum and maximum values. Annotators can select any value within the range, making this ideal for scoring dimensions like accuracy, quality, or relevance on a numeric scale: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#continuous
- [definition] Categorical — Categorical configs provide a discrete set of predefined options for annotators to choose from. Each category must have a `value` (a numeric identifier used for scoring and analytics) and a `label` (the text shown to annotators). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#categorical
- [definition] Freeform — Freeform configs allow annotators to provide open-ended text feedback without any predefined structure or constraints. This type has no `min`, `max`, or `categories` fields—annotators can enter any text they want. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/annotation-queues-sdk#freeform

## How to audit evaluator scores
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/audit-evaluator-scores>

- [definition] How to audit evaluator scores — LLM-as-a-judge evaluators don't always get it right. Because of this, it is often useful for a human to manually audit the scores left by an evaluator and correct them where necessary. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/audit-evaluator-scores#how-to-audit-evaluator-scores
- [definition] In the comparison view — In the comparison view, you may click on any feedback tag to bring up the feedback details. From there, click the "edit" icon on the right to bring up the corrections view. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/audit-evaluator-scores#in-the-comparison-view
- [definition] In the runs table — In the runs table, find the "Feedback" column and click on the feedback tag to bring up the feedback details. Again, click the "edit" icon on the right to bring up the corrections view. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/audit-evaluator-scores#in-the-runs-table
- [definition] In the SDK — Corrections can be made via the SDK's `update_feedback` function, with the `correction` dict. You must specify a `score` key which corresponds to a number for it to be rendered in the UI. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/audit-evaluator-scores#in-the-sdk

## Authentication methods
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/authentication-methods>

- [definition] Authentication methods — LangSmith supports multiple authentication methods for easy sign-up and login. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/authentication-methods#authentication-methods
- [definition] Email/Password — Users can use an email address and password to sign up and login to LangSmith. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/authentication-methods#emailpassword
- [definition] Social providers — Users can alternatively use their credentials from GitHub or Google. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/authentication-methods#social-providers
- [definition] SAML SSO — Enterprise customers can configure [SAML SSO](/langsmith/user-management) and [SCIM](/langsmith/user-management). [Get a demo](https://www.langchain.com/contact-sales) to learn more. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/authentication-methods#saml-sso
- [definition] Self-Hosted — Self-hosted customers have more control over how their users can login to LangSmith. For more in-depth coverage of configuration options, see [the self-hosting docs](/langsmith/self-hosted) and [Helm chart](https://github.com/langchain-ai/helm/tree/main/charts/langsmith). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/authentication-methods#self-hosted
- [definition] SSO with OAuth 2.0 and OIDC — Production installations should configure SSO in order to use an external identity provider. This enables users to login through an identity platform like Auth0/Okta. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/authentication-methods#sso-with-oauth-20-and-oidc
- [definition] Email/Password a.k.a. basic auth — This auth method requires very little configuration as it does not require an external identity provider. It is most appropriate to use for self-hosted trials. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/authentication-methods#emailpassword-aka-basic-auth
- [definition] None — This authentication mode will be removed after the launch of Basic Auth. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/authentication-methods#none

## Export trace data to BigQuery
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export>

- [snippet] 1. Create a GCS bucket: gcloud storage buckets create gs://YOUR_BUCKET_NAME \ — `gcloud storage buckets create gs://YOUR_BUCKET_NAME \` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#1-create-a-gcs-bucket
- [snippet] 2. Create a service account and grant access: gcloud iam service-accounts create langsmith-bulk-export \ — `gcloud iam service-accounts create langsmith-bulk-export \` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#2-create-a-service-account-and-grant-access
- [snippet] 2. Create a service account and grant access: gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://YOUR_BUCKET_NAME \ — `gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://YOUR_BUCKET_NAME \` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#2-create-a-service-account-and-grant-access
- [snippet] 3. Generate HMAC keys: gcloud storage hmac create \ — `gcloud storage hmac create \` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#3-generate-hmac-keys
- [snippet] 4. Create a bulk export destination: curl --request POST \ — `curl --request POST \` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#4-create-a-bulk-export-destination
- [snippet] 5. Create a bulk export job: curl --request POST \ — `curl --request POST \` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#5-create-a-bulk-export-job
- [snippet] 5. Create a bulk export job: curl --request POST \ — `curl --request POST \` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#5-create-a-bulk-export-job
- [snippet] Output file structure: gs://YOUR_BUCKET_NAME/YOUR_PREFIX/export_id=<uuid>/tenant_id=<uuid>/session_id=<uuid>/resource=runs/year=<year>/month=<m — `gs://YOUR_BUCKET_NAME/YOUR_PREFIX/export_id=<uuid>/tenant_id=<uuid>/session_id=<uuid>/resource=runs/` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#output-file-structure
- [snippet] Credential rotation: curl --request PATCH \ — `curl --request PATCH \` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#credential-rotation
- [parameter] `400 Access denied` on destination creation: Likely cause=HMAC credentials lack write permission; Fix=Verify the service account has `storage.objects.create` on the bucket — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#troubleshooting
- [parameter] `400 Key ID you provided does not exist`: Likely cause=HMAC access ID is invalid; Fix=Regenerate HMAC keys in GCP — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#troubleshooting
- [parameter] `400 Invalid endpoint`: Likely cause=Endpoint URL is malformed; Fix=Use exactly `https://storage.googleapis.com` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#troubleshooting
- [parameter] BigQuery table shows no rows: Likely cause=Export not yet complete; Fix=Check export status with `GET /api/v1/bulk-exports/{export_id}` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#troubleshooting
- [parameter] BigQuery partition pruning not working: Likely cause=Incorrect source URI prefix; Fix=Ensure the source URI prefix ends before the first partition key, e.g. `gs://BUCKET/PREFIX` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#troubleshooting
- [parameter] BigQuery picks up `tmp/` files: Likely cause=Broad file path glob; Fix=Use `export_id=*` in your file path instead of `*` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#troubleshooting
- [definition] 1. Create a GCS bucket — Create a dedicated GCS bucket for LangSmith exports. Using a dedicated bucket makes it easier to grant scoped permissions without affecting other data: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#1-create-a-gcs-bucket
- [definition] 2. Create a service account and grant access — Create a GCP service account that LangSmith will use to write data to GCS: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#2-create-a-service-account-and-grant-access
- [definition] 3. Generate HMAC keys — LangSmith connects to GCS using the S3-compatible XML API, which requires HMAC keys rather than a service account JSON key. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#3-generate-hmac-keys
- [definition] 4. Create a bulk export destination — Create a destination in LangSmith pointing to your GCS bucket. Set `endpoint_url` to `https://storage.googleapis.com` to use the GCS S3-compatible API. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#4-create-a-bulk-export-destination
- [definition] Temporary validation file — During destination creation (and [credential rotation](#credential-rotation)), LangSmith writes a temporary `.txt` file to `YOUR_PREFIX/tmp/` to verify write access, then attempts to delete it. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#temporary-validation-file
- [definition] 5. Create a bulk export job — Create an export targeting a specific project. Use `format_version: v2_beta` for BigQuery compatibility—it produces UTC timezone-aware timestamps that BigQuery handles correctly. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#5-create-a-bulk-export-job
- [definition] Output file structure — Exported files land in GCS using a Hive-partitioned path structure: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#output-file-structure
- [definition] 6. Load data into BigQuery — BigQuery offers two ways to access your exported data. Both require granting the BigQuery service account read access to your GCS bucket first. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#6-load-data-into-bigquery
- [definition] Credential rotation — To rotate your HMAC keys without interrupting active exports: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/big-query-bulk-export#credential-rotation

## BYOC architecture
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-architecture>

- [parameter] **Control plane**: Where it runs=LangChain's cloud, `us-east-2`; What it holds=Authentication, organization and workspace configuration, billing and usage metadata, LangSmith API keys, and the static frontend assets — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-architecture#control-plane-and-data-plane-model
- [parameter] **Data plane**: Where it runs=Your AWS account, in the region you choose; What it holds=Traces, prompts, datasets, evaluators, experiments, insights runs, annotation queues, agent deployments, workspace secrets, and other application data — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-architecture#control-plane-and-data-plane-model
- [definition] Control plane and data plane model — A BYOC deployment is split across two planes. This page describes the components of each plane, how they communicate, and what LangChain provisions in your account. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-architecture#control-plane-and-data-plane-model
- [definition] Provisioned resources — LangChain provisions the following in your account: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-architecture#provisioned-resources
- [definition] Cross-account IAM permissions — LangChain needs cross-account IAM permissions to provision and manage resources within your AWS account. These permissions let LangChain: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-architecture#cross-account-iam-permissions
- [definition] How least privilege is enforced — The role is scoped to only what BYOC operations require: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-architecture#how-least-privilege-is-enforced
- [definition] Data traffic — Sensitive data does not leave your VPC, and does not pass through LangChain's VPC. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-architecture#data-traffic
- [definition] Connectivity — All communication between the control plane and your data plane travels over AWS PrivateLink, in both directions. LangChain does not reach your environment over the public internet. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-architecture#connectivity
- [definition] DNS and ingress — Traffic reaches LangSmith through an Istio ingress fronted by an AWS NLB, using Route 53 for DNS resolution. Once your data plane is created, its API URL is listed under **Settings > Data Planes** in the LangSmith UI. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-architecture#dns-and-ingress

## BYOC billing
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing>

- [parameter] **Amazon EKS**: What it covers=The Kubernetes control plane for the data plane cluster; Billing basis=Per cluster-hour — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **Amazon EC2**: What it covers=Nodes running in the EKS cluster; Billing basis=Per instance-hour — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **Amazon RDS**: What it covers=Instances for relational workloads; Billing basis=Per instance-hour, including Multi-AZ, plus storage, backups, and snapshots — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **Amazon ElastiCache**: What it covers=Redis instance for caching and queueing workloads; Billing basis=Per node-hour — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **Amazon S3**: What it covers=Bucket for LangSmith workloads, ClickHouse backups and VPC flow logs; Billing basis=Storage, requests, and data transfer — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **Amazon EBS**: What it covers=Node root disks, and the volumes for ClickHouse storage; Billing basis=Per GB-month, plus provisioned IOPS and throughput above the gp3 baseline — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **Regional NAT gateway**: What it covers=Outbound egress from the private subnets; Billing basis=Per hour, plus data processed — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **Elastic Load Balancing**: What it covers=Two network load balancers: one in front of the Istio ingress, and one for the EKS API PrivateLink endpoint; Billing basis=Per NLB-hour, plus NLCUs — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **AWS PrivateLink**: What it covers=The interface VPC endpoints the data plane uses; Billing basis=Per interface endpoint per availability zone-hour, plus data processed — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **AWS Lambda and Amazon EventBridge**: What it covers=Reconciliation of the PrivateLink endpoints; Billing basis=Per invocation, and per event published — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **Amazon CloudWatch Logs**: What it covers=EKS control plane logs; Billing basis=Ingestion and storage — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **VPC flow logs**: What it covers=Delivery of flow logs to S3; Billing basis=Per GB delivered — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **Amazon Route 53**: What it covers=Private hosted zone; Billing basis=Per hosted zone-month, plus queries — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [parameter] **AWS Secrets Manager**: What it covers=RDS-generated master secrets, and the application secrets LangSmith references; Billing basis=Per secret-month, plus API calls — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [definition] Cost model — A BYOC deployment produces two separate bills: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#cost-model
- [definition] Billable AWS services — Every data plane creates the following resources in your account. AWS charges for them at its own rates, independently of your LangSmith contract. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#billable-aws-services
- [definition] Data transfer — There are a few data transfer cost drivers in BYOC: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#data-transfer
- [definition] Service limits — AWS enforces default quotas per region and per account. Defaults are often too low for production on new or lightly used accounts, so check the following before you deploy, and request increases where needed: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-billing#service-limits

- [parameter] Fleet: Agents, shared skills, MCP servers, integrations, auth providers, schedules, triggers, webhooks, usage limits, sandbox policies, and workspace secrets. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#supported-resources
- [parameter] Context Hub: Context Hub agents and skills, including files, repository metadata, commit history, and commit tags. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#supported-resources
- [definition] Migrate to BYOC — The [LangSmith data migration tool](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langsmith-data-migration-tool) copies data from an existing LangSmith Cloud organization or [self-hosted](/langsmith/self-hosted) instance into a BYOC data plane. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#migrate-to-byoc
- [definition] Supported resources — The tool migrates the following resources between a source instance and a destination data plane: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#supported-resources
- [definition] Install the tool — Install the latest release with `uv`, `uvx`, or `pip`. For the current install commands, see [Installation](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langsmith-data-migration-tool#installation). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#migrate-with-the-tool
- [definition] Create the destination workspaces — Workspace IDs differ between instances, so create the target workspaces in the data plane first. See the `Create workspaces` section of the [BYOC onboarding docs](/langsmith/byoc-onboarding). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#migrate-with-the-tool
- [definition] Create the destination tracing projects — The tool does not create tracing projects. Create the projects you need in the destination workspace before you migrate automation rules or charts, or those mappings have no target. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#migrate-with-the-tool
- [definition] Configure the connection details — Set the source and destination credentials and endpoints: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#migrate-with-the-tool
- [definition] Run the migration — Use the interactive wizard to walk through every resource type: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#migrate-with-the-tool
- [definition] Complete the Fleet manual steps — [Fleet](/langsmith/fleet/index) resources migrate with the `fleet` command, but some values cannot cross instances. Complete the following in the destination workspace after migration: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#complete-the-fleet-manual-steps
- [definition] Traces — The tool does not migrate traces. To keep historical traces beyond the lifecycle of your old instance, [bulk export](/langsmith/data-export) them to an S3-compatible bucket. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#traces
- [definition] Deployed agents — Redeploy agents that run on your existing instance into a workspace in the data plane. Use the LangSmith UI or the API. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#deployed-agents
- [definition] Insights reports — [Insights](/langsmith/insights) reports are not migrated across instances. To keep a report, open its details in the LangSmith UI and select **Download**. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-migration#insights-reports

## BYOC onboarding
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-onboarding>

- [definition] BYOC onboarding — Before you start, review the [prerequisites](/langsmith/byoc#prerequisites). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-onboarding#byoc-onboarding
- [definition] Enable BYOC on your organization — Create an organization in LangSmith on AWS at [aws.smith.langchain.com](https://aws.smith.langchain.com), or reuse an existing one. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-onboarding#byoc-onboarding
- [definition] Create the IAM role — Apply the [`langsmith-byoc-role` Terraform module](https://github.com/langchain-ai/terraform/tree/main/modules/byoc/aws/langsmith-byoc-role) in your AWS account. This creates the cross-account role LangChain assumes to provision and manage the data plane. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-onboarding#byoc-onboarding
- [definition] Create the data plane — Navigate to **Settings > Data Planes** and create a data plane with the following parameters: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-onboarding#byoc-onboarding
- [definition] Wait for provisioning — LangChain provisions the infrastructure on your behalf. The data plane moves from `Requested` to `Provisioning` to `Active`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-onboarding#byoc-onboarding
- [definition] Set up private connectivity — Data planes are provisioned with a private endpoint by default, so you need private connectivity to reach it, such as Tailscale, AWS PrivateLink, or VPC peering. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-onboarding#byoc-onboarding
- [definition] Create workspaces — A workspace named `dp-<data_plane_name>` is provisioned automatically inside the new data plane. It is not accessible until the data plane is reachable. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-onboarding#byoc-onboarding
- [definition] (Optional) Migrate existing data — If you are moving from an existing LangSmith Cloud or [self-hosted](/langsmith/self-hosted) instance, users, roles, datasets, prompts, experiments, annotation queue configuration, automation rules, dashboards, and Fleet resources can be copied over. Traces cannot be migrated today. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-onboarding#byoc-onboarding

## BYOC operations
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-operations>

- [definition] BYOC operations — LangChain operates your data plane after provisioning, including upgrades, scaling, monitoring, and security patching. Most maintenance is non-disruptive and requires no action from you. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-operations#byoc-operations
- [definition] Autoscaling — LangChain scales your data plane as load changes, so you do not need to size or tune it: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-operations#autoscaling
- [definition] High availability — Data planes are provisioned for high availability by default. The VPC spans the availability zones in your region, and RDS and ElastiCache run Multi-AZ with automatic failover. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-operations#high-availability
- [definition] Instance sizes — Data planes are provisioned with default instance sizes for the databases and node groups. To run a data plane on smaller instances, contact the LangChain team. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-operations#instance-sizes
- [definition] LangSmith upgrades — LangChain upgrades the LangSmith version in your data plane once a week. Upgrades are rolling, replica-by-replica, so there is no whole-service downtime. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-operations#langsmith-upgrades
- [definition] Supporting service upgrades — Background services such as Istio, KEDA, and the ClickHouse operator are upgraded on a regular cadence. These upgrades are non-intrusive, and no service interruption is expected. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-operations#supporting-service-upgrades
- [definition] Kubernetes cluster upgrades — The EKS cluster that hosts your data plane requires periodic upgrades to maintain security, compatibility, and access to new features. LangChain performs these upgrades proactively, ahead of AWS end-of-support dates, and coordinates the window with you. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-operations#kubernetes-cluster-upgrades
- [definition] Maintenance windows — Any maintenance or upgrade that could cause downtime, such as a restart of RDS or ElastiCache, happens in a scheduled maintenance window that LangChain coordinates with you in advance. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-operations#maintenance-windows
- [definition] Observability — You can deploy observability tooling into the cluster, such as a Datadog agent or an OpenTelemetry collector, and your own security monitoring agents, as long as they do not interfere with LangSmith workloads. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-operations#observability
- [definition] Troubleshooting — The LangChain team has no standing access to your data, and can only manage the infrastructure of your data plane. When troubleshooting requires access to data, there are two paths: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-operations#troubleshooting

## Why BYOC
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-why>

- [parameter] **Primary value**: BYOC=Customer-owned data plane with a managed LangSmith operating model; Self-hosted=Maximum control over the full LangSmith deployment — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-why#compare-byoc-and-self-hosted
- [parameter] **Time to value**: BYOC=Faster: provision the account and role, then LangChain provisions the supported data plane architecture; Self-hosted=Longer: you design, provision, connect, secure, and operate the full stack — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-why#compare-byoc-and-self-hosted
- [parameter] **Operations**: BYOC=LangChain owns more of the product operating model, upgrade path, and supportable infrastructure pattern; Self-hosted=You own deployment, upgrades, scaling, monitoring, and incident response for the full stack — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-why#compare-byoc-and-self-hosted
- [parameter] **Architecture**: BYOC=Standardized and close to LangChain SaaS production architecture; Self-hosted=More flexible, but easier to drift from supported patterns — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-why#compare-byoc-and-self-hosted
- [parameter] **Best fit**: BYOC=Teams that need data isolation and private networking, but do not want to operate every LangSmith component themselves; Self-hosted=Teams that require full-stack ownership, unsupported infrastructure patterns, or cannot use a managed control plane — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-why#compare-byoc-and-self-hosted
- [definition] Why BYOC — BYOC is for organizations that want the data ownership and network isolation of self-hosting, without spending engineering time building and operating the full LangSmith platform themselves. The data plane stays in your AWS account, and LangChain manages the LangSmith infrastructure. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-why#why-byoc
- [definition] Compare BYOC and self-hosted — The table below compares the two deployment models: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-why#compare-byoc-and-self-hosted
- [definition] Move from self-hosted to BYOC — You can move to BYOC from an existing self-hosted deployment. Traces are not migrated today, but users, roles, datasets, experiments, prompts, annotation queue configuration, automation rules, and dashboards can be copied over. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/byoc-why#move-from-self-hosted-to-byoc

## Use server-side caching
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching>

- [snippet] Quick start: from langgraph_sdk.cache import swr — `from langgraph_sdk.cache import swr` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#quick-start
- [snippet] Configure freshness: from datetime import timedelta — `from datetime import timedelta` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#configure-freshness
- [snippet] Use with Pydantic models: from pydantic import BaseModel — `from pydantic import BaseModel` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#use-with-pydantic-models
- [snippet] Cache auth credentials: from datetime import timedelta — `from datetime import timedelta` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#cache-auth-credentials
- [snippet] Inspect cache status: result = await swr("my-key", my_loader) — `result = await swr("my-key", my_loader)` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#inspect-cache-status
- [snippet] Inspect cache status: await result.mutate(new_value)  # update the cache with a new value — `await result.mutate(new_value)  # update the cache with a new value` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#inspect-cache-status
- [snippet] Low-level cache API: from datetime import timedelta — `from datetime import timedelta` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#low-level-cache-api
- [snippet] `cache_get`: async def cache_get(key: str) -> Any | None — `async def cache_get(key: str) -> Any | None` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#cache-get
- [snippet] `cache_set`: async def cache_set(key: str, value: Any, *, ttl: timedelta | None = None) -> None — `async def cache_set(key: str, value: Any, *, ttl: timedelta | None = None) -> None` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#cache-set
- [parameter] `fresh_for`: Default=`timedelta(0)`; Description=Duration to treat a cached value as fresh. During this window, `swr` returns the cached value with no revalidation. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#configure-freshness
- [parameter] `max_age`: Default=`timedelta(days=1)`; Description=Maximum lifetime of a cached entry. After this, `swr` blocks on the loader before returning. Capped at 1 day. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#configure-freshness
- [parameter] **Miss**: Condition=Key not in cache; Behavior=Awaits `loader()`, stores result, returns it. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#how-revalidation-works
- [parameter] **Fresh**: Condition=`age < fresh_for`; Behavior=Returns cached value, no revalidation. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#how-revalidation-works
- [parameter] **Stale**: Condition=`fresh_for <= age < max_age`; Behavior=Returns cached value immediately, triggers background refresh. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#how-revalidation-works
- [parameter] **Expired**: Condition=`age >= max_age`; Behavior=Awaits `loader()`, stores result, returns it. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#how-revalidation-works
- [parameter] `key`: Type=`str`; Default=required; Description=The cache key — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#cache-set
- [parameter] `value`: Type=`Any`; Default=required; Description=Value to cache. Must be JSON-serializable — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#cache-set
- [parameter] `ttl`: Type=`timedelta \| None`; Default=`None`; Description=Time-to-live. The server caps this at 1 day. `None` or zero defaults to 1 day — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#cache-set
- [definition] Use server-side caching — [Agent Server](/langsmith/agent-server) includes a built-in cache you can use inside your deployed graphs. Call `swr` with a key and a loader function, and the server caches the result, revalidates stale entries in the background, and returns fresh data on every read. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#use-server-side-caching
- [definition] Quick start — Pass a key and an async loader function. `swr` returns the cached value if available, or calls your loader to fetch it: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#quick-start
- [definition] Configure freshness — Control how long cached values are considered fresh and when they expire: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#configure-freshness
- [definition] Use with Pydantic models — Pass a `model` parameter to automatically serialize and deserialize Pydantic models: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#use-with-pydantic-models
- [definition] Cache auth credentials — You can cache credential validation in a [custom auth handler](/langsmith/custom-auth) to avoid hitting your identity provider on every request: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#cache-auth-credentials
- [definition] Inspect cache status — `swr` returns an `SWRResult` object with the value and cache status: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#inspect-cache-status
- [definition] Low-level cache API — For simple get/set caching without revalidation, use `cache_get` and `cache_set` directly: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/caching#low-level-cache-api

- [definition] Dataset Examples — On the **Datasets** page under the **Examples** tab, Chat helps you understand your dataset structure, browse examples, and identify data patterns. - [definition] Annotation Queues — In **Annotation Queues**, Chat helps you analyze runs before making annotation decisions. - [definition] Evaluators — In the **Evaluators** builder, Chat helps you write and refine evaluator logic. Chat can generate evaluator code, suggest improvements, and help you test your evaluator against examples. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/chat#evaluators

- [definition] Cloud platform features — This page describes the platform features that apply only to [Cloud](/langsmith/cloud) deployments. - [definition] Data region — Deployments can be created in two data regions: US and EU. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/cloud-platform-features#data-region
- [definition] Static IP addresses — All traffic from deployments created after January 6, 2025 comes through a NAT gateway. This NAT gateway has several static IP addresses depending on the data region. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/cloud-platform-features#static-ip-addresses
- [definition] Allowlist IP addresses — Use the following static IP addresses to allowlist traffic for each region: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/cloud-platform-features#allowlist-ip-addresses
- [definition] Payload size — The maximum payload size for all requests sent to Cloud deployments is 25 MB. A request with a payload larger than 25 MB returns a `413 Payload Too Large` error. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/cloud-platform-features#payload-size
- [definition] Deployment types — The control plane offers two deployment types: Serverless and Dedicated. Each is available in three sizes: Small, Medium, and Large. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/cloud-platform-features#deployment-types
- [definition] Serverless — Serverless deployments are cost-optimized for background and latency-tolerant agents, as well as development, testing, and preview branches. A Serverless deployment scales to zero after a period of inactivity and wakes on the next request. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/cloud-platform-features#serverless
- [definition] Dedicated — Dedicated deployments are always-on and built for production workloads in the critical path, such as customer-facing applications. Each Dedicated deployment has its own database with automatic backups and high availability, and autoscales across replicas as load increases. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/cloud-platform-features#dedicated
- [definition] Sizes — Both Serverless and Dedicated are available in three sizes: Small, Medium, and Large. Each size sets the compute and memory provisioned for a deployment, and larger sizes autoscale to more replicas. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/cloud-platform-features#sizes
- [definition] Database provisioning — The control plane and [data plane](/langsmith/data-plane) listener application coordinate to automatically create a Postgres database for each Cloud deployment. The database serves as the [persistence layer](/oss/python/langgraph/persistence#memory-store) for the deployment. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/cloud-platform-features#database-provisioning
- [definition] Scaling — Cloud deployments autoscale automatically; you do not configure queue workers, replicas, or pool sizes directly. A Dedicated deployment adds and removes replicas based on CPU utilization, memory utilization, and the number of pending runs, up to the maximum for its size. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/cloud-platform-features#scaling

- [parameter] **where_known**: Required whenever the runtime can expose the value. Omit only when the runtime genuinely cannot provide the information. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#availability-tiers
- [parameter] **contextual**: Optional metadata. Omit when not applicable. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#availability-tiers
- [parameter] `root`: The top-level run representing a full agent turn or session. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#run-types
- [parameter] `llm`: A language model call within a turn. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#run-types
- [parameter] `tool`: A tool invocation within a turn. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#run-types
- [parameter] `subagent`: A nested or delegated agent run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#run-types
- [parameter] `interrupted`: A run that was interrupted before completion. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#run-types
- [parameter] `ls_agent_version`: Tier=`where_known`; Description=Version string for the agent runtime, for example `"1.0.28"`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#all-run-types
- [parameter] `git_branch`: Tier=`where_known`; Description=Active Git branch in the repository being edited. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#all-run-types
- [parameter] `git_commit_sha`: Tier=`where_known`; Description=Full SHA of the current Git commit. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#all-run-types
- [parameter] `git_repo_url`: Tier=`where_known`; Description=Remote URL of the repository. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#all-run-types
- [parameter] `working_directory`: Tier=`where_known`; Description=Absolute path of the working directory. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#all-run-types
- [parameter] `ls_model_name`: Tier=`where_known`; Description=Model identifier, for example `"claude-opus-4-5"`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#llm-runs
- [parameter] `ls_provider`: Tier=`where_known`; Description=Model provider, for example `"anthropic"`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#llm-runs
- [parameter] `ls_tool_name`: Tier=`always`; Description=Name of the tool invoked, for example `"bash"` or `"computer"`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#tool-runs
- [parameter] `ls_subagent_id`: Tier=`always`; Description=Stable identifier for the subagent. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#subagent-runs
- [parameter] `ls_subagent_type`: Tier=`always`; Description=Type or role of the subagent, for example `"researcher"`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#subagent-runs
- [definition] Coding agent metadata contract — This schema is the authoritative contract for metadata that coding agents attach to LangSmith runs. It defines which fields are required on every run, which fields are expected when the runtime can supply them, and which fields apply only to specific run types. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#coding-agent-metadata-contract
- [definition] Supported integrations — The following integrations implement this schema: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#supported-integrations
- [definition] Global identity block — Every run type must include the following identity fields in its metadata: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#global-identity-block
- [definition] Availability tiers — Fields in this schema are marked with one of three availability tiers: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#availability-tiers
- [definition] Run types — This schema distinguishes five run types. Some fields apply only to a subset of run types. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#run-types
- [definition] All run types — The [global identity block](#global-identity-block) fields are **always** required on every run type. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#all-run-types
- [definition] `interrupted` runs — Interrupted runs carry the same fields as `root` runs. The run type itself signals the abnormal termination state; no additional required fields are added. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/coding-agent-metadata-contract#interrupted-runs

- [definition] Columns — Click the <Icon icon="columns-3"/> icon to show or hide individual feedback keys or metrics in the comparison view. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/compare-experiment-results#columns
- [definition] Table views — Select one of three table view icons at the top right of the comparison view: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/compare-experiment-results#table-views
- [definition] Display types — There are three built-in experiment views that cover several display types: **Default**, **YAML**, **JSON**. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/compare-experiment-results#display-types
- [definition] View regressions and improvements — In the comparison view, red highlights runs that *regressed* on any feedback key against your source experiment, while green highlights runs that *improved*. At the top of each feedback column, you can see how many runs did better or worse than your source experiment. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/compare-experiment-results#view-regressions-and-improvements
- [definition] View side-by-side diffs — When comparing two experiments, for JSON and YAML display styles, you can toggle on the experiment diff mode to compare experiment outputs. The diff mode highlights modifications between outputs, and can be particularly useful for structured output comparisons. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/compare-experiment-results#view-side-by-side-diffs
- [definition] Update source experiment and metric — To track regressions across experiments, you can: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/compare-experiment-results#update-source-experiment-and-metric
- [definition] Expand details panel — Click on any row to open a details panel for that example for the compared experiments. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/compare-experiment-results#expand-details-panel
- [definition] Use experiment metadata as chart labels — You can configure the x-axis labels for the charts based on [experiment metadata](/langsmith/filter-experiments-ui#background-add-metadata-to-your-experiments). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/compare-experiment-results#use-experiment-metadata-as-chart-labels

- [definition] Configure IAM authentication for data stores — Agent Server can use a cloud workload identity to generate short-lived PostgreSQL and Redis credentials at runtime. This removes static database and cache passwords from your deployment configuration. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/configure-iam-auth#configure-iam-authentication-for-data-stores
- [definition] Configure AWS — Agent Server uses the AWS SDK default credential chain to create RDS authentication tokens and ElastiCache SigV4 authentication tokens. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/configure-iam-auth#configure-aws
- [definition] Configure Azure — Agent Server uses `DefaultAzureCredential` to obtain Microsoft Entra tokens for PostgreSQL and Redis. - [definition] Configure GCP — Agent Server uses Google ADC to obtain Cloud SQL login tokens and Memorystore access tokens. ADC supports GKE Workload Identity Federation, attached service accounts, service account impersonation, and `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/configure-iam-auth#configure-gcp
- [definition] Configure the standalone Helm chart — For a [standalone Agent Server deployment](/langsmith/deploy-standalone-server) on Kubernetes, set the provider selectors on every Agent Server workload. If the separate queue deployment is enabled, configure the API and queue deployments with the same identity and environment variables. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/configure-iam-auth#configure-the-standalone-helm-chart

<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/configure-ttl>

- [definition] Configuring thread and checkpoint TTL — Checkpoints capture the state of conversation threads. Setting a TTL automatically deletes or prunes expired data. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/configure-ttl#configuring-thread-and-checkpoint-ttl
- [definition] Configuring store item TTL — Store items allow cross-thread data persistence. Configuring TTL for store items helps manage memory by removing stale data. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/configure-ttl#configuring-store-item-ttl
- [definition] Combining TTL configurations — You can configure TTLs for both checkpoints and store items in the same `langgraph.json` file to set different policies for each data type. Here is an example: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/configure-ttl#combining-ttl-configurations

- [definition] Runtime overrides — For store items, pass `ttl` to `put` to override the default lifespan. Pass `refresh_ttl` to `get` or `search` to control whether reads refresh expiration. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/configure-ttl#runtime-overrides
- [definition] Deployment process — After configuring TTLs in `langgraph.json`, deploy or restart your LangGraph application for the changes to take effect. Use [`langgraph dev`](/langsmith/local-dev-testing#langgraph-dev) for local development or [`langgraph up`](/langsmith/local-dev-testing#langgraph-up) for Docker deployment. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/configure-ttl#deployment-process

## Context engineering concepts
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/context-engineering-concepts>

- [definition] Context engineering concepts — Agents behave inconsistently in production when their context is poorly managed. _Context_ is the information an agent relies on to act, such as system instructions, tool definitions, and reference material. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/context-engineering-concepts#context-engineering-concepts
- [definition] Skills — A _skill_ is a versioned repo in the Context Hub that packages a reusable capability an agent can invoke. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/context-engineering-concepts#skills
- [definition] Agents — An _agent_ is an AI system that completes tasks end to end using tools, skills, and subagents. An _agent repo_ packages its configuration, including high-level instructions, linked skills and subagents, and tool configuration. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/context-engineering-concepts#agents
- [definition] Choose between skills and agents — Skills are reusable context modules. Agent repos are top-level bundles that define how an agent should operate. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/context-engineering-concepts#choose-between-skills-and-agents
- [definition] Linked repos — Context Hub commits support three entry types in `files`: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/context-engineering-concepts#linked-repos
- [definition] Context Hub vs. store backend — Context in LangSmith can be managed by two different backends: the **Context Hub** and a **store backend**. They serve different purposes, and most agents use both. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/context-engineering-concepts#context-hub-vs-store-backend
- [definition] Versioning — Every change to a repo in the **Context Hub** creates a new commit. Commits are immutable, browsable, and comparable, so you can: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/context-engineering-concepts#versioning
- [definition] Sharing and permissions — The **Context Hub** is designed for teams. Every repo lives in a [workspace](/langsmith/administration-overview#workspaces), and access depends on workspace permissions plus repo visibility: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/context-engineering-concepts#sharing-and-permissions
