- [definition] Manual instrumentation — If you trace without one of the wrappers in [Supported integrations](#supported-integrations) (for example, emitting runs through `RunTree`, the REST API, or a custom wrapper around a provider SDK), set `ls_message_format` on each LLM run's metadata to route the trace to the correct extractor: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/messages-view-integrations#manual-instrumentation

Members without it see the OAuth fields disabled, with a masked secret hint. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/model-configurations#configure-oauth-on-a-model-configuration
- [definition] Edit semantics — OAuth fields follow edit behaviors that protect the stored secret: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/model-configurations#edit-semantics
- [definition] How a request flows — When a request runs against an OAuth-enabled configuration, LangSmith mints a bearer through an internal broker, caches the result, and stamps the bearer on every outbound LLM call until the cached token expires. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/model-configurations#how-a-request-flows
- [definition] Fallback behavior — If the broker cannot mint a token (IdP unreachable, credentials invalid, configuration deleted between request preparation and execution), the request falls back to the static workspace API key for the provider. If no workspace key is set, expect a provider 401 on the outbound call. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/model-configurations#fallback-behavior
- [definition] Surface coverage — OAuth-enabled configurations are honored wherever model configurations are consumed: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/model-configurations#surface-coverage

## Include multimodal content in a prompt

- [definition] Include multimodal content in a prompt — Some applications are based around multimodal content, like a chatbot that can answer questions about a PDF or image. In these cases, you'll want to include multimodal content in your prompt and test the model's ability to answer questions about the content. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/multimodal-content#include-multimodal-content-in-a-prompt
- [definition] Inline content — Click the file icon in the message where you want to add multimodal content. Under the `Upload content` tab, you can upload a file and include it inline in the prompt. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/multimodal-content#inline-content
- [definition] Template variables — Click the file icon in the message where you want to add multimodal content. Under the `Template variables` tab, you can create a template variable for a specific attachment type. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/multimodal-content#template-variables
- [definition] Populate the template variable — Once you've added a template variable, you can provide content for it using the panel on the right side of the screen. Simply click the `+` button to upload or select content that will be used to populate the template variable. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/multimodal-content#populate-the-template-variable
- [definition] Run an evaluation — After testing out your prompt manually, you can [run an evaluation](/langsmith/evaluate-with-attachments?mode=ui) to see how the prompt performs over a golden dataset of examples. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/multimodal-content#run-an-evaluation

## Troubleshoot trace nesting
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/nest-traces>

- [snippet] To resolve: import asyncio — `import asyncio` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/nest-traces#to-resolve
- [snippet] To resolve: import asyncio — `import asyncio` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/nest-traces#to-resolve
- [snippet] To resolve: import asyncio — `import asyncio` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/nest-traces#to-resolve
- [snippet] To resolve: from langsmith.utils import ContextThreadPoolExecutor — `from langsmith.utils import ContextThreadPoolExecutor` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/nest-traces#to-resolve
- [snippet] To resolve: from langsmith import traceable, get_current_run_tree — `from langsmith import traceable, get_current_run_tree` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/nest-traces#to-resolve
- [definition] Troubleshoot trace nesting — When tracing with the LangSmith SDK, LangGraph, and LangChain, tracing should automatically propagate the correct context so that code executed within a parent trace will be rendered in the expected location in the UI. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/nest-traces#troubleshoot-trace-nesting
- [definition] Python — The following outlines common causes for "split" traces when building with python. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/nest-traces#python
- [definition] Context propagation using asyncio — When using async calls (especially with streaming) in Python versions < 3.11, you may encounter issues with trace nesting. This is because Python's `asyncio` only [added full support for passing context](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html#asyncio.create_task) in version 3.11. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/nest-traces#context-propagation-using-asyncio
- [definition] Context propagation using threading — It's common to start tracing and want to apply some parallelism on child tasks all within a single trace. Python's stdlib `ThreadPoolExecutor` by default breaks tracing. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/nest-traces#context-propagation-using-threading

## Observability concepts
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts>

- [parameter] Shape: Trace=Tree of runs; Thread=Sequence of traces; Trajectory=Flat, ordered list of messages — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#compare-traces-threads-and-trajectories
- [parameter] Contains: Trace=Every run, with full inputs and outputs; Thread=Every run in every linked trace; Trajectory=Every message in every linked trace, deduplicated — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#compare-traces-threads-and-trajectories
- [parameter] Reach for it when: Trace=You are debugging why one operation failed or ran slow; Thread=You are inspecting how the agent behaved across turns, with timing and nesting intact; Trajectory=You are reading what was exchanged in the session, without the execution detail — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#compare-traces-threads-and-trajectories
- [definition] Observability concepts — LangSmith Observability lets you record, inspect, and analyze every step your AI agent takes. This page explains how that data is structured and visualized in LangSmith as well as how to start sending traces. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#observability-concepts
- [definition] How LangSmith structures and visualizes data — In LangSmith, every unit of work an agent performs, such as a model call, tool invocation, or information retrieval, is recorded as a [_run_](#runs). The runs for a single operation are collected into a [_trace_](#traces). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#how-langsmith-structures-and-visualizes-data
- [definition] Runs — A _run_ represents a single unit of work executed by an agent, such as calling an LLM, formatting a prompt, or retrieving documents. If you are familiar with [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/), you can think of a run as a span. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#runs
- [definition] Traces — A _trace_ is a collection of runs for a single operation. For example, if a user request triggers an agent that calls a model, runs a tool, and then calls the model again, all of those runs belong to the same trace. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#traces
- [definition] Threads — A _thread_ is a sequence of traces representing a single multi-turn session. A turn is one exchange in that session: a user's message and everything the agent does in response. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#threads
- [definition] Trajectories — A _trajectory_ is a flat, ordered list of messages that shows the path an agent took from start to finish. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#trajectories
- [definition] Projects — A _project_ is a container for all the traces related to a single application or service. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#projects
- [definition] Feedback — _Feedback_ allows you to score an individual run based on certain criteria. Each feedback entry consists of a tag and a score, and is bound to a run by a unique run ID. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#feedback
- [definition] Tags — _Tags_ are strings you can attach to runs to categorize, filter, and group them in the LangSmith UI. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#tags
- [definition] Metadata — _Metadata_ is a collection of key-value pairs you can attach to runs. For example, application version, environment, or any other contextual information. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#metadata
- [definition] Sending traces — There are two ways to send trace data to LangSmith. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#sending-traces
- [definition] Integrations — LangSmith _integrations_ provide automatic tracing for popular LLM providers and agent frameworks (the equivalent of auto-instrumentation in general observability). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#integrations
- [definition] Manual instrumentation — _Manual instrumentation_ lets you add tracing to any code, regardless of the framework. Use it when you're not using a supported integration or when you need granular control over what gets traced. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#manual-instrumentation
- [definition] Data retention — LangSmith (SaaS) retains trace data for 180 days from ingestion. After that, traces are permanently deleted, with limited metadata retained for usage statistics. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/observability-concepts#data-retention

- [snippet] Configure the collector: receivers: — `receivers:` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/otel-gateway-trace-redaction#configure-the-collector

- [definition] Prerequisites — Both of the following approaches require the following environment variables. Set `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` to the address of your collector: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/otel-gateway-trace-redaction#prerequisites
- [definition] Configure the collector — Both approaches also require an OpenTelemetry collector running as an intermediary between your application and LangSmith. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/otel-gateway-trace-redaction#configure-the-collector
- [definition] Trace with LangChain, LangGraph, or Deep Agents — Use this approach if your application already uses [LangChain](/langsmith/trace-with-langchain), [LangGraph](/langsmith/trace-with-langgraph), or [Deep Agents](/langsmith/trace-deep-agents). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/otel-gateway-trace-redaction#trace-with-langchain-langgraph-or-deep-agents
- [definition] Trace with the OpenTelemetry SDK directly — Use this approach if you need programmatic control over the tracer provider and exporter. For example, to set per-request project names or configure custom headers at runtime. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/otel-gateway-trace-redaction#trace-with-the-opentelemetry-sdk-directly

- [definition] Collect feedback with presigned URLs — Presigned feedback tokens let you collect [feedback](/langsmith/observability-concepts#feedback) from client-side applications (browsers, mobile apps, etc.) without exposing your [LangSmith API key](/langsmith/create-account-api-key). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/presigned-feedback-tokens#collect-feedback-with-presigned-urls
- [definition] Create a presigned feedback token — Use [`create_presigned_feedback_token()`](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langsmith/client/Client/create_presigned_feedback_token) / [`createPresignedFeedbackToken`](https://reference.langchain.com/javascript/classes/langsmith.client.Client.html#createpresignedfeedbacktoken) to generate a… — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/presigned-feedback-tokens#create-a-presigned-feedback-token
- [definition] Set token expiration — Tokens expire after 3 hours by default. Pass `expiration` to customize this with either a `timedelta` (relative) or a `datetime` (absolute): — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/presigned-feedback-tokens#set-token-expiration
- [definition] Constrain feedback values — Pass `feedback_config` to restrict what values clients can submit. This is useful for enforcing a specific feedback schema (e.g., thumbs up/down, 1–5 stars, or categorical labels): — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/presigned-feedback-tokens#constrain-feedback-values
- [definition] Create tokens in batch (Python only) — Use `create_presigned_feedback_tokens` (plural) to generate tokens for multiple feedback keys in a single call: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/presigned-feedback-tokens#create-tokens-in-batch-python-only
- [definition] Submit feedback with a presigned URL — Once you have a presigned URL, your frontend code or email client submits feedback by sending a `POST` or `GET` request to it. The URL does not require an API key or authentication because the token provides the authorization. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/presigned-feedback-tokens#submit-feedback-with-a-presigned-url
- [definition] POST request — Use `POST` from your frontend when a user interacts with a feedback control (e.g., clicking a thumbs up button). `POST` supports `score`, `value`, `comment`, `correction`, and `metadata` fields. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/presigned-feedback-tokens#post-request
- [definition] GET request — Use `GET` when embedding a feedback link in an email or Slack message. The user's click triggers the request. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/presigned-feedback-tokens#get-request
- [definition] Submit feedback using the SDK — You can also submit feedback from a presigned token using the SDK, which is useful for server-side workflows where you received a token URL from another service. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/presigned-feedback-tokens#submit-feedback-using-the-sdk
- [definition] List existing tokens — Retrieve all presigned feedback tokens for a run using `list_presigned_feedback_tokens` / `listPresignedFeedbackTokens`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/presigned-feedback-tokens#list-existing-tokens

## Preview builds
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/preview-builds>

- [definition] Preview builds — Preview builds create temporary **preview deployments** for pull requests. Use a preview deployment to test Agent Server changes in isolation before you merge them into the branch that runs your parent deployment. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/preview-builds#preview-builds
- [definition] Manage secrets — A preview deployment inherits the parent deployment's secrets when LangSmith creates it. You can override the inherited secrets on the preview deployment. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/preview-builds#manage-secrets
- [definition] Delete preview deployments — LangSmith deletes a preview deployment when its idle TTL expires. You can also delete it manually at any time. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/preview-builds#delete-preview-deployments

- [parameter] Authentication: Constructor API key, then `LANGSMITH_API_KEY`, then profile OAuth access token, then profile `api_key`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/profile-configuration#override-profile-values

- [definition] Profile configuration — LangSmith SDK profiles let you keep [API keys](/langsmith/create-account-api-key), endpoints, and workspace IDs in a reusable JSON file instead of setting the same environment variables in every shell session. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/profile-configuration#profile-configuration
- [definition] Minimum versions — Profile support is available in the following releases: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/profile-configuration#minimum-versions

- [definition] Authenticate with `langsmith auth login` — Run `langsmith auth login` to authenticate with OAuth instead of manually creating an API-key profile. - [definition] Override profile values — Explicit client constructor arguments and environment variables take precedence over profile values. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/profile-configuration#override-profile-values

- [definition] Mount profiles in remote runtimes — For remote runtimes, mount the profile file as a secret file and set `LANGSMITH_CONFIG_FILE` to the mounted path. Do not copy the file into the image or repository. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/profile-configuration#mount-profiles-in-remote-runtimes
- [definition] Docker — Mount your local profile directory into the container: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/profile-configuration#docker

- [definition] Remote development and CI — In remote development environments or CI jobs, store the profile JSON in the platform's secret store, write it to a temporary file at runtime, and set `LANGSMITH_CONFIG_FILE` to that file path. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/profile-configuration#remote-development-and-ci

## Prompt engineering concepts
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts>

- [snippet] Prompts vs. prompt templates: You are a customer support agent. This is the refund policy: — `You are a customer support agent. This is the refund policy:` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#prompts-vs-prompt-templates
- [snippet] Prompts vs. prompt templates: { — `{` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#prompts-vs-prompt-templates
- [snippet] Prompts vs. prompt templates: You are a customer support agent. This is the refund policy: — `You are a customer support agent. This is the refund policy:` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#prompts-vs-prompt-templates
- [definition] Prompt engineering concepts — While traditional software applications are built by writing code, AI applications often derive their logic from prompts. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#prompt-engineering-concepts
- [definition] Why prompt engineering? — A prompt guides the model's behavior without changing its underlying capabilities. By providing instructions, examples, and context, prompts shape how the model responds to inputs. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#why-prompt-engineering
- [definition] Prompt types — There are two different types of prompt formats: `chat` style prompts and `completion` style prompts. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#prompt-types
- [definition] Prompts vs. prompt templates — While _prompt_ and _prompt template_ are often used interchangeably, understanding the distinction helps clarify how LangSmith manages and evaluates your AI application. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#prompts-vs-prompt-templates
- [definition] Prompts in LangSmith — You can store and version prompt templates in LangSmith. These templates can be tested in the Playground, versioned with commits and tags, and pulled into your application code. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#prompts-in-langsmith
- [definition] F-string vs. mustache — You can format your prompt template with input variables using either [f-string](https://realpython.com/python-f-strings/) or [mustache](https://mustache.github.io/mustache.5.html) format. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#f-string-vs-mustache
- [definition] Tools — [Tools](/langsmith/use-tools) are interfaces the LLM can use to interact with the outside world. Tools consist of a name, description, and JSON schema of arguments used to call the tool. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#tools
- [definition] Structured output — Structured output is a feature of most state of the art LLMs, wherein instead of producing raw text as output they stick to a specified schema. This may or may not use [Tools](#tools) under the hood. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#structured-output
- [definition] Model — Optionally, you can store a model configuration alongside a prompt template. This includes the name of the model and any other parameters (temperature, etc). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#model
- [definition] Prompt versioning — Versioning is a key component of iterating on and collaborating with prompts. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#prompt-versioning
- [definition] Commits — Every saved update to a prompt creates a new commit with a unique commit hash. This allows you to: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#commits
- [definition] Tags — Commit tags are human-readable labels that point to specific commits in your prompt's history. Unlike commit hashes, tags can be moved to point to different commits, allowing you to update which version your code references without changing the code itself. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#tags
- [definition] Playground — The Playground provides an interface for iterating on and testing prompts. You can access the Playground from the sidebar or directly from a saved prompt. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#playground
- [definition] Testing multiple prompts — You can add multiple prompts to your Playground to compare outputs and evaluate performance: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#testing-multiple-prompts
- [definition] Testing over a dataset — To test over a dataset, select the dataset from the top right and click Start. You can configure whether results are streamed and the number of repetitions for the test. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#testing-over-a-dataset

- [parameter] **f-string**: Syntax=`{variable}`; Best for=Simple prompts with basic variable substitution — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#prompt-template-format-guide
- [parameter] **mustache**: Syntax=`{{variable}}`; Best for=Complex prompts with loops, conditionals, nested data, or evaluators — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#prompt-template-format-guide
- [definition] Prompt template format guide — This page describes the [prompt template](/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#prompts-vs-prompt-templates) formats supported in the [Playground](/langsmith/prompt-engineering-concepts#playground), [prompt hub](/langsmith/manage-prompts#public-prompt-hub), and… — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#prompt-template-format-guide
- [definition] F-string syntax — F-string templates use Python-style formatting with single curly braces `{variable}`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#f-string-syntax
- [definition] Basic variables — Variables are replaced with their values from the input data. Variable names must match exactly (case-sensitive): — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#basic-variables
- [definition] Variable names — F-string variable names are treated as simple string identifiers. They cannot contain dots, brackets, or special characters—just alphanumeric characters and underscores. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#variable-names
- [definition] Literal braces — Sometimes you need to include actual curly braces in your output (for example, in JSON examples or code snippets). To do this, **double the braces**: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#literal-braces
- [definition] Limitations — LangSmith's f-string implementation is limited to keep templates simple and predictable. The following features are **not supported**: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#limitations
- [definition] Mustache syntax — [Mustache](https://mustache.github.io/mustache.5.html) is a "logic-less" templating language, meaning it doesn't allow arbitrary code execution but does provide structured control flow through sections. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#mustache-syntax
- [definition] Basic variables — Like f-strings, mustache replaces variables with their values: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#basic-variables
- [definition] Nested object access — You can traverse nested objects using dot notation: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#nested-object-access
- [definition] Sections — Sections are mustache's core feature. A section starts with `{{#name}}` and ends with `{{/name}}`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#sections
- [definition] Nested loops — You can nest sections to handle multi-level data structures: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#nested-loops
- [definition] Array elements by index — Sometimes you need a specific element rather than looping. Use dot notation with numeric indices: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#array-elements-by-index
- [definition] Conditionals — You can use sections as conditionals. They only render if the value exists, is non-empty, and is not `false`: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#conditionals
- [definition] Inverted sections — Inverted sections render only when a value doesn’t exist, is false, null, undefined, or an empty array. Inverted sections are commonly used to handle empty states, such as missing data or empty lists. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#inverted-sections
- [definition] Comments — Comments document your templates without affecting output. Use `{{! — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#comments
- [definition] Special variables for evaluators and threads — When building [evaluators](/langsmith/evaluation-concepts#evaluators) or working with conversational AI, LangSmith automatically provides special variables that structure conversation data in useful ways. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#special-variables-for-evaluators-and-threads
- [definition] Thread message variables — LangSmith provides three pre-structured views of conversation [threads](/langsmith/evaluation-concepts#threads): — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#thread-message-variables
- [definition] Example with thread context — The following example is a practical evaluator prompt that uses thread context: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#example-with-thread-context
- [definition] Few-shot examples — Few-shot prompting teaches the LLM by example. You provide several input-output pairs demonstrating the task, then ask it to perform the same task on new input. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#few-shot-examples
- [definition] Few-shot placeholder — In LangSmith, use the `{{few_shot_examples}}` placeholder where you want your examples to appear: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/prompt-template-format#few-shot-placeholder

- [definition] How to run evaluations with pytest — The LangSmith pytest plugin lets Python developers define their datasets and evaluations as pytest test cases. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#how-to-run-evaluations-with-pytest
- [definition] Installation — This functionality requires Python SDK version `langsmith>=0.3.4`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#installation
- [definition] Define and run tests — The pytest integration lets you define datasets and evaluators as test cases. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#define-and-run-tests
- [definition] Log inputs, outputs, and reference outputs — Every time we run a test we're syncing it to a dataset example and tracing it as a run. There's a few different ways that we can trace the example inputs and reference outputs and the run outputs. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#log-inputs-outputs-and-reference-outputs
- [definition] Log feedback — By default LangSmith collects the pass/fail rate under the `pass` feedback key for each test case. You can add additional feedback with `log_feedback`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#log-feedback
- [definition] Trace intermediate calls — LangSmith will automatically trace any traceable intermediate calls that happen in the course of test case execution. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#trace-intermediate-calls
- [definition] Grouping tests into a test suite — By default, all tests within a given file will be grouped as a single "test suite" with a corresponding dataset. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#grouping-tests-into-a-test-suite
- [definition] Naming experiments — You can name an experiment using the `LANGSMITH_EXPERIMENT` env var: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#naming-experiments
- [definition] Experiment metadata — You can attach custom metadata to the experiment (project) created by each test run. This is useful for tracking which model, prompt version, or environment was used for a given experiment. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#experiment-metadata
- [definition] Caching — LLMs on every commit in CI can get expensive. To save time and resources, LangSmith lets you cache HTTP requests to disk. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#caching
- [definition] pytest features — `@pytest.mark.langsmith` is designed to stay out of your way and works well with familiar `pytest` features. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#pytest-features
- [definition] Parametrize with `pytest.mark.parametrize` — You can use the `parametrize` decorator as before. This will create a new test case for each parametrized instance of the test. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#parametrize-with-pytestmarkparametrize
- [definition] Parallelize with `pytest-xdist` — You can use [pytest-xdist](https://pytest-xdist.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) as you normally would to parallelize test execution: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#parallelize-with-pytest-xdist
- [definition] Async tests with `pytest-asyncio` — `@pytest.mark.langsmith` works with sync or async tests, so you can run async tests exactly as before. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#async-tests-with-pytest-asyncio
- [definition] Watch mode with `pytest-watch` — Use watch mode to quickly iterate on your tests. We *highly* recommend only using this with test caching (see below) enabled to avoid unnecessary LLM calls: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#watch-mode-with-pytest-watch
- [definition] Rich outputs — If you'd like to see a rich display of the LangSmith results of your test run you can specify `--langsmith-output`: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#rich-outputs
- [definition] Dry-run mode — If you want to run the tests without syncing the results to LangSmith, you can set `LANGSMITH_TEST_TRACKING=false` in your environment. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#dry-run-mode
- [definition] Expectations — LangSmith provides an [expect](https://reference.langchain.com/python/langsmith/observability/sdk/expect/) utility to help define expectations about your LLM output. For example: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/pytest#expectations

- [parameter] [`name=`](#name): Sets the agent and default deployment name — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#define-an-agent
- [parameter] [`model=`](#model): Selects the chat model — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#define-an-agent
- [parameter] [`tools=`](#tools): Adds tools the agent can call — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#define-an-agent
- [parameter] [`middleware=`](#middleware): Adds behavior around model calls, tool calls, and the agent lifecycle — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#define-an-agent
- [parameter] [`subagents=`](#subagents): Defines specialized agents for delegated tasks — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#define-an-agent
- [parameter] [`permissions=`](#permissions): Controls path-level access for filesystem tools — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#define-an-agent
- [parameter] [`interrupt_on=`](#human-in-the-loop): Pauses before selected tool calls for human approval — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#define-an-agent
- [parameter] [`response_format=`](#structured-output): Defines a structured output schema — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#define-an-agent
- [definition] Define a Managed Deep Agent — The agent definition selects the model and core capabilities of a Managed Deep Agent. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#define-a-managed-deep-agent
- [definition] Project structure — The agent entry lives at the project root: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#project-structure
- [definition] Name — `name` is required. Pass a static string that starts with a letter and contains only letters, numbers, underscores, or hyphens, such as `"research-assistant"`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#name
- [definition] Model — Set `model` to the chat model the agent uses. The simplest option is a `provider:model` string. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#model
- [definition] Use LLM Gateway — You can use [LLM Gateway](langsmith/llm-gateway) to control rate limits, fallbacks, and more. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#use-llm-gateway
- [definition] Tools — Pass tools in the `tools` list to let the agent call application logic or external services. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#tools
- [definition] Middleware — Pass middleware in the `middleware` list to add behavior around model calls, tool calls, and the agent lifecycle. Middleware runs in list order. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#middleware
- [definition] Subagents — Pass subagent definitions in `subagents` when the agent should delegate specialized or context-heavy work. Each subagent can have its own prompt, model, and tools. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#subagents
- [definition] Permissions — Pass filesystem permission rules in `permissions` to control which paths the agent's built-in filesystem tools can read or write. See [Permissions](/oss/python/deepagents/permissions). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#permissions
- [definition] Human-in-the-loop — Set `interrupt_on` to pause before selected tool calls. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#human-in-the-loop
- [definition] Structured output — Set `response_format` when the agent must return data that matches a schema instead of an unconstrained text response. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-agent-definition#structured-output

- [definition] Deploy the agent — During deployment, Managed Deep Agents provisions your agent in Slack from the channel declaration. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels-slack#deploy-the-agent
- [definition] Deploy your agent — Run the deployment command from the project root: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels-slack#deploy-the-agent
- [definition] Authorize Slack if prompted — If you haven't authorized LangSmith before, the CLI displays an HTTPS authorization link. Open the link, select the Slack workspace, and approve the requested access. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels-slack#deploy-the-agent
- [definition] Use the agent in Slack — After the first deployment, your agent sends you a direct message in Slack. Reply to the message to start an agent run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels-slack#deploy-the-agent

## Connect Managed Deep Agents to channels
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels>

- [snippet] Project structure: my-agent/ — `my-agent/` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels#project-structure
- [snippet] Understand channels: flowchart LR — `flowchart LR` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels#understand-channels
- [definition] Connect Managed Deep Agents to channels — A channel makes a managed deep agent available in an external messaging service. Messages from the service can start agent runs, and the agent's final responses return through the same service. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels#connect-managed-deep-agents-to-channels
- [definition] Project structure — Channel declarations live in the project-level `channels/` directory: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels#project-structure
- [definition] Understand channels — A channel combines three parts of an external messaging integration: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels#understand-channels
- [definition] Declare channels in a project — Put each channel in a separate module under `channels/`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels#declare-channels-in-a-project
- [definition] Distinguish channels from connectors — A channel receives messages that start agent runs and delivers responses. An [MCP connector](/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-mcp-connectors) gives the agent tools from a remote MCP server. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-channels#distinguish-channels-from-connectors

- [parameter] `--follow`: Keep streaming new logs. This is the default in an interactive terminal. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-cli#read-deployment-logs
- [parameter] `--no-follow`: Print recent logs and exit. This is the default when output is piped. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-cli#read-deployment-logs
- [parameter] `--workspace-id WORKSPACE_ID`: Workspace ID to read from. Overrides `LANGSMITH_WORKSPACE_ID`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-cli#read-deployment-logs

- [parameter] `--yes`: Delete without asking for confirmation. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-cli#delete-deployments

- [parameter] Deploy fails with 401 or 403: Confirm the API key belongs to a workspace with beta access. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-cli#troubleshooting
- [parameter] Deploy reports a missing model provider API key: Add the provider key, such as `OPENAI_API_KEY`, to `.env`, export it in your shell, or configure it as a LangSmith workspace secret. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-cli#troubleshooting
- [parameter] Deploy reports a Context Hub conflict: The Context Hub repo changed during deploy. Re-run `mda deploy`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-cli#troubleshooting

- [parameter] Deployment reaches `BUILD_FAILED` or `DEPLOY_FAILED`: Open the printed deployment URL in LangSmith and inspect the revision logs. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-cli#troubleshooting

- [parameter] **Instructions and skills**: Role=Deploy-owned agent behavior; Scope=Shared by the deployment and read-only to the agent — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-memory#memory-compared-to-related-state
- [parameter] **Thread state**: Role=Conversation continuity; Scope=One thread — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-memory#memory-compared-to-related-state

- [definition] Add memory to Managed Deep Agents — Normally, a managed deep agent's conversational memory is scoped to a thread or session. - [definition] Project structure — The optional memory declaration lives at the project root: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-memory#project-structure
- [definition] Enable memory — Export a named `memory` declaration with the `"agent"` scope: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-memory#enable-memory
- [definition] How the agent uses memory — Enabling memory mounts one Context Hub tree, `memories/agent`, at `/memories/agent/` in the agent filesystem: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-memory#how-the-agent-uses-memory
- [definition] How the agent decides what to remember — The agent decides what to remember based on prompting. To make the policy explicit, add guidance like the following to `instructions.md` and adapt it to your application: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-memory#how-the-agent-decides-what-to-remember
- [definition] Distinguish instructions from memory — `instructions.md` defines how the agent should behave. Memory stores knowledge the agent learns and uses across threads. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-memory#distinguish-instructions-from-memory

- [definition] Add a sandbox to Managed Deep Agents — Agents often want to write or execute code when doing their job. A sandbox gives a managed deep agent an isolated filesystem and shell for working with files, running code, and executing commands. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-sandboxes#add-a-sandbox-to-managed-deep-agents
- [definition] Project structure — Keep the agent entry point at the project root and the sandbox declaration under `sandbox/`. Add `sandbox/setup.sh` only if you want to provision a snapshot: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-sandboxes#project-structure
- [definition] Configure a sandbox — `mda init` scaffolds a sandbox declaration. Managed Deep Agents enables the sandbox only while the `sandbox/` directory is present. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-sandboxes#configure-a-sandbox
- [definition] Provision a snapshot — If `sandbox/setup.sh` exists, `mda deploy` and `mda dev` run the script once and save the resulting environment as a snapshot. Modifications from that run, such as cloned repositories and installed packages, persist in the snapshot. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-sandboxes#provision-a-snapshot
- [definition] Choose a bake base — With no bake base, LangSmith's default sandbox template is the starting point. To start from something else, set exactly one of these: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-sandboxes#choose-a-bake-base
- [definition] How the agent uses the sandbox — The agent uses filesystem tools such as `ls`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit_file`, `delete`, `glob`, and `grep`, and runs shell commands with `execute`. Use `instructions.md` to specify where the agent should work and what it must not modify. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-sandboxes#how-the-agent-uses-the-sandbox
- [definition] Sandbox lifecycle — Managed Deep Agents owns sandbox naming, recipe bake, reuse, recovery, and cleanup. Each durable thread gets its own sandbox, cloned from the current recipe snapshot. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-sandboxes#sandbox-lifecycle

- [definition] How skills compare to other concepts — Skills is context that is loaded dynamically, when the agent chooses to. The agent cannot modify them. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/python/managed-deep-agents-skills#how-skills-compare-to-other-concepts

## Role-based access control
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac>

- [parameter] [Organization Admin](#organization-admin): Full permissions to manage organization configuration, users, billing, and workspaces — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#organization-roles
- [parameter] [Organization Operator](#organization-operator): Management access to workspaces and users for day-to-day operations, excluding admin-level privileges — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#organization-roles
- [parameter] [Organization User](#organization-user): Read access to organization information and ability to create personal access tokens — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#organization-roles
- [parameter] [Organization Viewer](#organization-viewer): Read-only access to organization information — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#organization-roles
- [parameter] [Workspace Admin](#workspace-admin): Full permissions for all resources, including workspace settings and member management — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#workspace-roles
- [parameter] [Workspace Editor](#workspace-editor): Full permissions for most resources, cannot manage workspace settings or delete certain resources — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#workspace-roles
- [parameter] [Workspace Viewer](#workspace-viewer): Read-only access to all workspace resources — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#workspace-roles
- [definition] Role-based access control — This reference explains LangSmith's Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) system for managing organization-level and workspace-level permissions. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#role-based-access-control
- [definition] Organization roles — Organization roles are **distinct from the workspace RBAC feature** and are used to manage organization-wide capabilities. The roles are system-defined and cannot be modified or extended. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#organization-roles
- [definition] Workspace roles — Workspace roles are part of the **Enterprise RBAC feature** and control what users can do with resources inside a workspace: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#workspace-roles
- [definition] Creating custom roles — Custom roles are created at the [organization](/langsmith/administration-overview#organizations) level and can be assigned to users in any [workspace](/langsmith/administration-overview#workspaces) within that organization. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#creating-custom-roles
- [definition] Understand permission behavior — Some permissions offer granular control when used in custom roles: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rbac#understand-permission-behavior

## Release stages
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-stages>

- [parameter] [Alpha](#alpha): Availability=Design partners only; Changes=Breaking changes expected; the feature may change significantly or never ship; Self-hosted / BYOC=Not guaranteed; Support=No formal SLA — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-stages#release-stages
- [parameter] [Beta](#beta): Availability=Public or a private group; Changes=Interface or behavior may still change; GA expected within a few months; Self-hosted / BYOC=Typically added during beta; Support=Actively maintained; SLA varies by feature — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-stages#release-stages
- [parameter] [GA](#generally-available-ga): Availability=Public; Changes=Stable; breaking changes require a deprecation period; Self-hosted / BYOC=Supported; Support=Fully supported — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-stages#release-stages
- [definition] Release stages — LangSmith ships features through three release stages: alpha, beta, and generally available (GA). Each stage sets a consistent expectation for how stable a feature is, where it runs, and how it is supported, so you can decide when to adopt it. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-stages#release-stages
- [definition] Alpha — Alpha is the earliest release stage, used to validate a feature with a small audience before wider release. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-stages#alpha
- [definition] Beta — Beta makes a feature available for real use while its interface and behavior are being finalized. Beta features are functional end to end, not partial implementations, so you can adopt them in production workflows and help shape them before general availability. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-stages#beta
- [definition] Generally available (GA) — GA features are stable and fully supported for production use. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-stages#generally-available-ga

## Release policy
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions>

- [parameter] Preview: Published mirroring the LangSmith SaaS release cadence — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions#release-cadence
- [parameter] Stable: new major (`v0.X.0`): Approximately every 6 weeks (two per quarter) — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions#release-cadence
- [parameter] Stable: patch (`v0.X.Y`): Weekly (typically Friday), skipped if no changes. Ad-hoc releases issued for critical customer issues. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions#release-cadence
- [parameter] Stable: Chart version=`0.15.17`; LangSmith version=`0.15.24` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions#version-numbering
- [parameter] Preview (release candidate): Chart version=`0.16.0-rc.15`; LangSmith version=`0.16.19rc1` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions#version-numbering
- [definition] Release policy — Self-hosted LangSmith ships on two release channels: a stable channel that customers run in production, and a preview channel that tracks the next major version. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions#release-policy
- [definition] Stable — The current generally available major version. LangSmith recommends this channel for production. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions#stable
- [definition] Preview — The development build of the next major version. Preview includes new features and fixes as they merge into LangSmith SaaS, so you can evaluate the next major version before it becomes stable. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions#preview
- [definition] Version numbering — Every self-hosted release has two version numbers: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions#version-numbering
- [definition] Version support — LangSmith supports the current stable major version (`N`) and the previous stable major version (`N-1`): — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions#version-support
- [definition] Current version — To check the current stable and preview versions, refer to the [self-hosted changelog](/langsmith/self-hosted-changelog). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/release-versions#current-version

## Set up automation rules
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rules>

- [definition] Set up automation rules — While you can manually sift through and process production logs from your LLM application, it often becomes difficult as your application scales to more users. LangSmith provides **Automations** that allow you to trigger certain actions on your trace data. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rules#set-up-automation-rules
- [definition] How automation rules execute — Each automation rule runs on an independent polling schedule. If you have multiple rules on the same project, a webhook rule may process a run before an evaluator rule has scored it, or vice versa. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rules#how-automation-rules-execute
- [definition] Set the item type to runs or threads — The **Item Type** control determines what a rule matches. Set it to **Runs** and the rule evaluates each matching run as it arrives. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rules#set-the-item-type-to-runs-or-threads
- [definition] Configure a thread rule — Selecting **Threads** changes three parts of the rule form: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rules#configure-a-thread-rule
- [definition] Set the thread idle time — A thread rule acts only after the thread goes idle. Once the last trace in a thread is ingested, LangSmith waits for the tracing project's configured idle time to elapse, which signals that the conversation is complete. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rules#set-the-thread-idle-time
- [definition] Extend data retention for a thread — [Data retention](/langsmith/usage-and-billing#data-retention-auto-upgrades) is a property of a trace, not of a thread. When a thread rule has **Extend Data Retention** enabled, it upgrades **every trace in the matched thread** to extended retention, not only the most recent one. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rules#extend-data-retention-for-a-thread
- [definition] View automation rules — In the [UI](https://smith.langchain.com?utm_source=docs&utm_medium=cta&utm_campaign=langsmith-signup&utm_content=langsmith-rules), navigate to **Tracing** in the sidebar and select a tracing project. To view existing automation rules for that tracing project, click on the **Automations** tab. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rules#view-automation-rules
- [definition] Create a rule — 1. In the [UI](https://smith.langchain.com?utm_source=docs&utm_medium=cta&utm_campaign=langsmith-signup&utm_content=langsmith-rules), navigate to **Tracing** in the sidebar and select a tracing project. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rules#create-a-rule
- [definition] View logs for your automations — Logs allow you to gain confidence that your rules are working as expected. You can view logs for your automations by navigating to the **Automations** tab within a tracing project and clicking the **Logs** button for the rule you created. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/rules#view-logs-for-your-automations

- [parameter] **`id`**: Type=UUID; Description=Unique identifier for the span. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`name`**: Type=string; Description=The name associated with the run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`inputs`**: Type=object; Description=A map of inputs provided to the run. For runs with `run_type='llm'`, this typically contains a `messages` array of message objects sent to the model. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`run_type`**: Type=string; Description=[Type of run](#run-types), for example, `'llm'`, `'chain'`, `'tool'`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`start_time`**: Type=datetime; Description=Start time of the run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`end_time`**: Type=datetime; Description=End time of the run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`extra`**: Type=object; Description=Any extra information run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`error`**: Type=string; Description=Error message if the run encountered an error. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`outputs`**: Type=object; Description=A map of outputs generated by the run. For runs with `run_type='llm'`, this typically contains a `messages` array of message objects returned by the model. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`events`**: Type=array of objects; Description=A list of event objects associated with the run. This is relevant for runs executed with streaming. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`tags`**: Type=array of strings; Description=Tags or labels associated with the run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`trace_id`**: Type=UUID; Description=Unique identifier for the trace the run is a part of. This is also the `id` field of the root run of the trace — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`dotted_order`**: Type=string; Description=[Ordering string](#what-is-dotted_order), hierarchical. Format: `<run_start_time>Z<run_uuid>`.`<child_run_start_time>Z<child_run_uuid>`... — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`status`**: Type=string; Description=Current status of the run execution, e.g., `'error'`, `'pending'`, `'success'` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`child_run_ids`**: Type=array of UUIDs; Description=List of IDs for all child runs. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`direct_child_run_ids`**: Type=array of UUIDs; Description=List of IDs for direct children of this run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`parent_run_ids`**: Type=array of UUIDs; Description=List of IDs for all parent runs. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`feedback_stats`**: Type=object; Description=Aggregations of feedback statistics for this run — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`reference_example_id`**: Type=UUID; Description=ID of a reference example associated with the run. This is usually only present for evaluation runs. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`total_tokens`**: Type=integer; Description=Total number of tokens processed by the run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`prompt_tokens`**: Type=integer; Description=Number of tokens in the prompt of the run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`completion_tokens`**: Type=integer; Description=Number of tokens in the completion of the run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`total_cost`**: Type=decimal; Description=Total cost associated with processing the run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`prompt_cost`**: Type=decimal; Description=Cost associated with the prompt part of the run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format
- [parameter] **`completion_cost`**: Type=decimal; Description=Cost associated with the completion of the run. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/run-data-format#run-span-data-format

## Set a sampling rate for traces
<https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sample-traces>

- [snippet] Set a global sampling rate: export LANGSMITH_TRACING_SAMPLING_RATE=0.75 — `export LANGSMITH_TRACING_SAMPLING_RATE=0.75` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sample-traces#set-a-global-sampling-rate
- [snippet] Set different sampling rates per client: from langsmith import Client, tracing_context — `from langsmith import Client, tracing_context` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sample-traces#set-different-sampling-rates-per-client
- [definition] Set a sampling rate for traces — When working with high-volume applications, you may not want to log every trace to LangSmith. Sampling rates allow you to control what percentage of traces are logged, helping you balance observability needs with cost considerations. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sample-traces#set-a-sampling-rate-for-traces
- [definition] Set a global sampling rate — This section is relevant for those using the [LangSmith SDK](/langsmith/reference) or [LangChain](/oss/python/langchain/overview), not for those logging directly with the LangSmith API. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sample-traces#set-a-global-sampling-rate
- [definition] Set different sampling rates per client — You can also set sampling rates on specific `Client` instances and use the [`tracing_context`](/langsmith/annotate-code#use-the-trace-context-manager-python-only) context manager: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sample-traces#set-different-sampling-rates-per-client
- [definition] Sampling or conditional tracing — Sampling provides **probabilistic** control over trace volume, while [conditional tracing](/langsmith/conditional-tracing) provides **deterministic** control based on business logic. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sample-traces#sampling-or-conditional-tracing

- [snippet] Example: curl -X POST "$LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT/v2/sandboxes/boxes" \ — `curl -X POST "$LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT/v2/sandboxes/boxes" \` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#example
- [snippet] Python: from langsmith.sandbox import SandboxClient — `from langsmith.sandbox import SandboxClient` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#configure-via-sdk
- [snippet] TypeScript: import { SandboxClient } from "langsmith/sandbox"; — `import { SandboxClient } from "langsmith/sandbox";` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#configure-via-sdk
- [parameter] `allow_list`: **Default-deny.** Only listed destinations are reachable—including HTTP/HTTPS. If you set an `allow_list`, you must also list every HTTP(S) host the sandbox needs. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#allow-and-deny-lists
- [parameter] `deny_list`: **Default-allow for HTTP/HTTPS.** All HTTP(S) hosts remain reachable except those listed. A `deny_list` cannot open raw TCP ports. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#allow-and-deny-lists
- [parameter] `host`: Bare host → ports **80 and 443 only** (HTTP/S). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#pattern-syntax
- [parameter] `host:PORT`: Host on exactly `PORT`. `:22` grants only 22, **not** additive with 80/443—list the host twice if you need both. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#pattern-syntax
- [parameter] `*.example.com`: Glob (RFC 1034-style). The apex (`example.com`) is **not** included. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#pattern-syntax
- [parameter] `~regex`: Opaque regex match; no port suffix parsing. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#pattern-syntax
- [parameter] `1.2.3.4` / `10.0.0.0/8`: Literal IP or CIDR. CIDRs **cannot** carry a port (HTTP/S only in allow mode; block all ports in deny mode). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#pattern-syntax
- [parameter] `[::1]:22`: IPv6 literal uses the bracketed form when specifying a port. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#pattern-syntax
- [parameter] `match_hosts`: Hosts to intercept (supports globs like `*.github.com`) — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#configure-auth-proxy-rules
- [parameter] `match_paths`: Paths to match (empty = all paths) — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#configure-auth-proxy-rules
- [parameter] `headers`: Headers to inject, each with a `name`, `type`, and `value` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#configure-auth-proxy-rules
- [parameter] `env_vars`: Environment variables to set in the sandbox while the rule is enabled — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#configure-auth-proxy-rules
- [parameter] `no_proxy`: Hosts to bypass the proxy entirely (e.g. `localhost`) — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#configure-auth-proxy-rules
- [parameter] `workspace_secret`: References a workspace secret using `{KEY}` syntax. Resolved when the proxy configuration is applied. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#header-types
- [parameter] `plaintext`: Value is stored and returned as-is. Use for non-sensitive headers. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#header-types
- [parameter] `opaque`: Write-only. Value is encrypted at rest and never returned via the API. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#header-types
- [parameter] `api.github.com`: `Authorization: Bearer <github-token>` for `gh` and REST API calls — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#github-example
- [parameter] `github.com`, `*.github.com`: `Authorization: Basic <base64("x-access-token:<github-token>")>` for Git over HTTPS operations like clone, fetch, and push — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#github-example
- [parameter] `match_hosts`: Hosts to intercept (same syntax as rules; supports globs like `*.github.com`). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#callback-credential-example
- [parameter] `url`: Your callback endpoint. Must be an `http://` or `https://` URL reachable from the proxy. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#callback-credential-example
- [parameter] `request_headers`: Headers attached to the proxy → callback request, e.g., an HMAC or shared secret your endpoint uses to verify the request. Only `plaintext` and `opaque` types are permitted (no `workspace_secret`). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#callback-credential-example
- [parameter] `ttl_seconds`: How long resolved headers are cached before re-invoking the callback. Must be between 60 and 3600. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#callback-credential-example
- [definition] Sandbox auth proxy — The auth proxy lets sandbox code call external APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, GitHub, etc.) without hardcoding credentials. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#sandbox-auth-proxy
- [definition] Egress and network access control — The same `proxy_config` that injects credentials also controls which destinations a sandbox can reach. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#egress-and-network-access-control
- [definition] Default egress posture — By default (no `access_control` configured): — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#default-egress-posture
- [definition] Allow and deny lists — Add an `access_control` object to `proxy_config` with **either** an `allow_list` **or** a `deny_list` (not both—the request is rejected if both are set): — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#allow-and-deny-lists
- [definition] Pattern syntax — Each `allow_list`/`deny_list` entry uses the following forms: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#pattern-syntax
- [definition] Connecting to a database (raw TCP) — To let sandbox code reach an external PostgreSQL database with `psql`, `dbt`, or any driver, allow-list the host on its port. Because `allow_list` is default-deny, also list any HTTP(S) hosts the sandbox needs: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#connecting-to-a-database-raw-tcp
- [definition] Configure auth proxy rules — Add a `proxy_config` when creating a sandbox, or update an existing sandbox by patching its `proxy_config`. Each rule specifies: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#configure-auth-proxy-rules
- [definition] Header types — Each header has a `type` that controls how its value is stored and displayed: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#header-types
- [definition] Set environment variables from a rule — A rule's `env_vars` are plaintext environment variables set for every command in the sandbox while that rule is enabled. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#set-environment-variables-from-a-rule
- [definition] Authenticate AWS requests — Use an AWS auth rule when sandbox code needs to call AWS services with an AWS SDK or CLI. The proxy keeps the real AWS credentials outside the sandbox, then signs supported outbound HTTPS requests with AWS SigV4. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#authenticate-aws-requests
- [definition] Authenticate GCP requests — Use a GCP auth rule when sandbox code needs to call Google APIs with Google SDKs or CLIs. The proxy keeps the service account JSON outside the sandbox, then authenticates supported outbound HTTPS requests to Google API hosts matched by the sandbox proxy. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#authenticate-gcp-requests
- [definition] Single API example — Create a sandbox that automatically injects an OpenAI API key into outbound requests: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#single-api-example
- [definition] Multiple API example — Add multiple rules to authenticate with several services at once: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#multiple-api-example
- [definition] GitHub example — [Open SWE](https://github.com/langchain-ai/open-swe/blob/main/agent/integrations/langsmith.py) authenticates GitHub access by minting a short-lived GitHub App installation token outside the sandbox, then patching the sandbox with write-only `opaque` proxy rules. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#github-example
- [definition] Callback credential example — Static `workspace_secret` rules pull credentials from your workspace when the proxy configuration is applied, and `opaque` rules let your application patch in short-lived credentials such as the [GitHub token example](#github-example). — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#callback-credential-example
- [definition] Callback contract — The proxy makes the following request whenever it needs to resolve credentials for a matched host on a cache miss: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#callback-contract
- [definition] Example — Use a callback when your OAuth tokens are minted on demand by your own service: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-auth-proxy#example

- [definition] Sandbox CLI — The [LangSmith CLI](/langsmith/langsmith-cli) includes sandbox commands for creating snapshots, booting sandboxes, running commands, opening interactive shells, and tunneling TCP connections into a sandbox. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-cli#sandbox-cli
- [definition] End-to-end workflow — Create a sandbox, then run commands inside it: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-cli#end-to-end-workflow
- [definition] Manage sandboxes — Create a sandbox with the default runtime. Add `--snapshot-id` only when you want to boot from a reusable custom snapshot: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-cli#manage-sandboxes
- [definition] Proxy configuration — Use `--proxy-config @proxy.json` on `create` or `update` to configure the sandbox auth proxy. Prefer workspace secrets for credential injection instead of placing raw secrets in local files. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-cli#proxy-configuration
- [definition] Run commands — Use `sandbox exec` for one-off commands: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-cli#run-commands
- [definition] Open an interactive console — Use `sandbox console` for a PTY-backed interactive shell: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-cli#open-an-interactive-console
- [definition] Tunnel TCP ports — Use `sandbox tunnel` when you need a local TCP port that forwards to a service listening inside the sandbox. This is useful for databases, language servers, custom protocols, or local tools that expect `localhost`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-cli#tunnel-tcp-ports
- [definition] Set up SSH access — Use `sandbox ssh-setup` to configure standard SSH tools such as `ssh`, `scp`, `rsync`, and `sftp` through a sandbox tunnel. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-cli#set-up-ssh-access

- [parameter] GCS bucket prefix: `/mnt/mounts/eval-datasets` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-mounts#configure-mount-paths
- [parameter] Git repository: `/mnt/mounts/repo` — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-mounts#configure-mount-paths
- [parameter] `max_size_bytes`: Optional maximum size, in bytes, for the local mount cache. Set a positive value to add an explicit cap; omit it to leave the runtime default. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-mounts#cache-bucket-mounts
- [parameter] `writeback_seconds`: Optional delay, in seconds, before cached writes are written back to the bucket. The default is `0`. Lower values make writes visible to the bucket sooner; higher values can reduce write traffic for workloads that rewrite the same files. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-mounts#cache-bucket-mounts
- [definition] Sandbox mounts — Sandbox mounts attach external data sources to a sandbox filesystem when the sandbox is created. Use mounts when sandbox code needs direct file access to object storage buckets or public Git repositories without copying the data into the sandbox image. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-mounts#sandbox-mounts
- [definition] Configure mount paths — Each mount has an `id`, a `type`, and a `mount_path` / `mountPath`. Mount paths must be absolute paths under `/mnt/mounts`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-mounts#configure-mount-paths
- [definition] Mount an S3 bucket — S3 mounts require AWS auth. The SDK creates an AWS auth proxy rule from `aws_auth` / `awsAuth`, so the sandbox can access the bucket without seeing the real access keys. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-mounts#mount-an-s3-bucket
- [definition] Mount a GCS bucket — GCS mounts require GCP auth. The OAuth scope is supplied by the backend, derived from the mounts themselves: read-only mounts get `devstorage.read_only` and writable mounts get `devstorage.read_write`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-mounts#mount-a-gcs-bucket
- [definition] Mount a public Git repository — Public Git mounts do not require AWS or GCP auth. Use an HTTPS remote URL and optionally pin a branch or tag. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-mounts#mount-a-public-git-repository
- [definition] Combine mounts — A sandbox can mount multiple sources. Build one `mount_config` / `mountConfig` with all mount specs, and include provider auth for every bucket provider used by those specs. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-mounts#combine-mounts
- [definition] Cache bucket mounts — S3 and GCS mounts support optional cache settings. Cache settings tune the local VFS cache used by the bucket mount; the bucket remains the source of truth. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-mounts#cache-bucket-mounts

- [parameter] CPU: Default=0.5 vCPU; Range=0.05 to 16 vCPU. Use `cpu_millicores` for sub-core requests (`500` is 0.5 vCPU); it takes precedence over `vcpus`. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-sdk#size-a-sandbox
- [parameter] Memory: Default=4 GiB per vCPU; Range=Up to 64 GiB. Must stay within 50% of the per-vCPU target, so a 1 vCPU sandbox accepts 2 to 6 GiB. Set memory without CPU and the CPU is derived from the same ratio. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-sdk#size-a-sandbox
- [parameter] Filesystem: Default=Snapshot capacity; Range=Up to 64 GiB, and never smaller than the snapshot it boots from. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-sdk#size-a-sandbox
- [parameter] `idle_ttl_seconds`: What it controls=The launcher stops the sandbox after this many seconds of inactivity. Any command execution or file I/O resets the timer. `0` disables the idle stop.; When it fires=Default `600` (10 minutes) when omitted. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-sdk#sandbox-lifetime-and-retention
- [parameter] `delete_after_stop_seconds`: What it controls=Once the sandbox enters the `stopped` state, this timer starts. The repo's latest commit tree is mirrored into the mount path and kept in sync for the sandbox's lifetime, so a new commit shows up in the running sandbox without a restart. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-sdk#mount-a-context-hub-repo
- [definition] Size a sandbox — Pass `vcpus`, `mem_bytes`, and `fs_capacity_bytes` (`vCpus`, `memBytes`, `fsCapacityBytes` in TypeScript) to size a sandbox at creation. Omit them and the sandbox gets the defaults below. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-sdk#size-a-sandbox

- [definition] Command lifecycle and TTL — The sandbox daemon manages command session lifecycles with two timeout mechanisms: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-sdk#command-lifecycle-and-ttl
- [definition] Service URLs (Python) — Access an HTTP service running inside a sandbox via an authenticated URL. You can open it in a browser, call it from code, or share it with a teammate. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-sdk#service-urls-python
- [definition] TCP tunnels (Python) — Access any TCP service running inside a sandbox as if it were local. The tunnel opens a local TCP port and forwards connections through a WebSocket to the target port inside the sandbox. — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-sdk#tcp-tunnels-python

- [definition] Use your own HTTP client — If you prefer a different HTTP client, use the raw URL and token: — https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/sandbox-service-urls#use-your-own-http-client
- [definition] Open in a browser — Use `browser_url` to open the service in a browser.
